articles.title_orig: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.title_zh: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.content_orig:
A gathering of World Council of Churches (WCC) commissions and reference groups on Life, Justice and Peace opened in Chiang Mai, where ecumenical leaders will explore what “ Being Church in the World Today” means.
Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, general secretary of the World Council of Churches adressed the Joint Conference of WCC Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice and Peace on the openning day of the conference in Chiang Mai, Thailand, 5 October 2026.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, in his opening address, offered a WCC perspective on ecclesiology, mission, witness, and hope.
“ Humanity faces wars and armed conflicts, growing inequalities, displacement and migration, ecological destruction, technological disruption, artificial intelligence, religious and political polarization, declining confidence in institutions, and profound questions concerning human dignity and the future of life itself,” he said. “ At the same time, Christianity itself is experiencing major transformations.”
The church is God's before it is ours, reflected Pillay. “ Here unity is not an ecclesial luxury,” he said. “ It is related directly to Christian witness.”
He further noted that a divided church struggles to proclaim a reconciled Christ. “ This is particularly important for the ecumenical movement,” he said. “ The WCC ’ s understanding of unity cannot be reduced to organizational uniformity.”
Dr Prawate Khid-arn, assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations of the Church of Christ in Thailand, prayed that the meeting will renew people ’ s hearts, deepen their commitment, and give them fresh energy and courage for the journey ahead.
“ May our discussions lead not only to words and recommendations, but also to meaningful actions that bring hope to those who suffer, restore human dignity, strengthen justice, care for God's creation, and contribute to genuine and lasting peace,” said Khid-arn. “ May the Holy Spirit guide your conversations, inspire your discernment, and strengthen our common witness.”
Rev. Grace Moon, general secretary of Christian Conference of Asia, noted the context of the meeting in Asia—a region full of spiritual richness, cultural diversity, and resilience, yet also a place where many still face challenges like inequality, displacement, violence, discrimination, and climate change.
“ Our Christian faith means we cannot ignore suffering or injustice—we are called to stand with those who are hurting, excluded, or silenced,” said Moon. “ We cannot solve these problems alone.”
Moon further noted that climate injustice, conflict, and discrimination are all connected. “ Our calling goes beyond charity—it is about working together for justice, healing, and the well-being of all people and creation,” said Moon.
The conference marks the second time that WCC commissions related to the Life, Justice, and Peace programme are meeting - the first such gathering was held in Geneva in 2024.
The first day of the conference currently underway began with pilgrimage encounters, giving participants an opportunity to meet local communities and organizations in and around Chiang Mai working on issues including clean air, migration, HIV and health justice, and interfaith dialogue.

articles.title_orig: California woman accused of spying on Taiwan president's family for China arrested at LAX
articles.title_zh: California woman accused of spying on Taiwan president's family for China arrested at LAX
articles.content_orig:
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said
US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on ​Sunday, accusing her of spying on the son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China , the agency said in a ⁠statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled a ​son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the ‌FBI alleged. The agency ‌did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report ‌identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s alleged actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to ‌a request for comment.
The Justice Department alleged Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and licence plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family.
Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection ⁠and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, ​the first assistant US ​attorney for the Central District of ​California, alleged in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang ​had a defence attorney. She ‌will appear on ​Monday in a ​Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as ​Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.

articles.title_orig: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.title_zh: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination” .
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates , where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

articles.title_orig: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.title_zh: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.content_orig:
The day before Cabrini Day, Archbishop James Golka made his first official visit to Mother Cabrini Shrine, celebrating a saint whose courage, compassion and missionary faith still challenge Catholics today.
There are certain days at Mother Cabrini Shrine when the past and present seem to come together in a particularly meaningful way. This Cabrini Day is one of them.
As Mother Cabrini Shrine celebrated Colorado’s Frances Xavier Cabrini Day, the Shrine also welcomed Archbishop James Golka for his first official visit — a fitting occasion for the new Archbishop of Denver to visit the holy ground dedicated to a woman whose faith, courage and missionary spirit left such a lasting mark on Colorado.
For Mother Cabrini Shrine, Cabrini Day is much more than a date on the calendar. It is an opportunity to remember the remarkable woman who first came to Denver in 1902 and whose footsteps eventually led her into the foothills west of the city. It was here that Mother Cabrini walked, prayed and cared for the girls from the Queen of Heaven Orphanage. More than a century later, pilgrims continue to come to this same holy ground seeking prayer, peace, healing and a deeper encounter with God.
In 2020, Colorado established Frances Xavier Cabrini Day as a state holiday, observed on the first Monday in October. It became the first paid state holiday in the nation named in honor of a woman — a remarkable distinction and a recognition of the impact Mother Cabrini’s life and work had on Colorado.
But the significance of Cabrini Day extends beyond remembering what Mother Cabrini accomplished more than a century ago. Her life continues to offer an example for the Church and the world today.
Mother Cabrini was a woman of extraordinary faith, but she was also a woman of action. She saw a need and responded. She crossed oceans, overcame obstacles and went wherever she believed God was calling her. Again and again, she said yes — to God, to those who needed her and to the mission placed before her.
(Photo by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
That message was echoed by Archbishop Golka during his homily at the 11:00 a.m. Mass.
Reflecting on Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life and witness, he said: “If the world had 100 more Mother Cabrinis, the faith and the Church would grow in ways that could hardly be imagined.”
He described Mother Cabrini as a woman who had the heart of a mother, caring deeply for those in need and offering an incredible example of faith lived through service. He also spoke about the importance of seeking the intercession of Mother Cabrini and all the saints, expressing his hope that pilgrims who come to the Shrine experience her intercession in their own lives and emphasizing that her witness remains as important today as it was during her lifetime.
That relevance was especially evident as the archbishop referenced “A Pilgrim People, A Shared Home,” an interfaith letter released in conjunction with Cabrini Day, affirming the dignity of every human life, with particular attention to migrant brothers and sisters. The message carries special significance on a day honoring Mother Cabrini, the patron saint of immigrants, whose ministry was shaped by her determination to accompany immigrants and others who found themselves vulnerable or in need.
More than a century later, the circumstances may be different, but Mother Cabrini’s example continues to call people to recognize the dignity of those around them and to respond with compassion.
After Mass, Mother Cabrini Shrine hosted a Festival of Nations that featured traditional music, dance and food from around the world. (Photos by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
Following Mass, Archbishop Golka greeted the faithful before joining the Shrine community for the Festival of Nations. The celebration was filled with joy and color, with foods representing cultures from around the world, people dressed in traditional clothing, and music and dance, including traditional Matachines dancing.
The celebration of nations is especially fitting on Cabrini Day. Mother Cabrini’s own life crossed borders, cultures and languages, and her mission was rooted in welcoming and caring for people far from home. More than a century later, the many cultures gathered together at the Shrine offered a beautiful reflection of both the universality of the Church and the mission she began.
Archbishop Golka’s first official visit was also a reminder that Mother Cabrini Shrine remains very much alive. Her mission continues through the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the clergy who serve the Shrine, its staff and volunteers, and the countless pilgrims who make their way to this holy ground each year. The life and ministry of a place like Mother Cabrini Shrine are sustained by many hands, many hearts and a shared commitment to carrying the mission forward.
Cabrini Day offers an opportunity not only to celebrate Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life, but also to consider what her example asks of all of us today.
Mother Cabrini saw those who were struggling and moved toward them. She trusted deeply in the Heart of Jesus, relied on prayer and refused to let seemingly insurmountable obstacles keep her from the work God had placed before her.
As Archbishop Golka reminded those gathered at the Shrine, the Church still needs Mother Cabrini. And perhaps one of the greatest ways to honor her is to continue the mission she so courageously began.
For those who have never visited Mother Cabrini Shrine — or perhaps have not been in many years — Cabrini Day offers a wonderful invitation to come and discover the woman behind the name. Walk where she walked, pray where she prayed, learn her story and discover why, more than a century later, St. Frances Xavier Cabrini and her mission still have so much to say to the world today.

articles.title_orig: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.title_zh: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.content_orig:
As a new parasite with flesh-eating larvae threatens the nation's livestock industry, a team of Virginia Tech researchers will be on the frontlines of defense.
Led by Luis Escobar, an associate professor of fish and wildlife conservation, the team is working on one of 40 breakthrough projects funded through the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to develop an integrated preparedness and response system against the re-emergence of the new world screwworm in the Americas.
“Preventing a screwworm invasion protects food production, food prices, rural economies, family farms, wildlife populations, companion animals such as dogs and horses, and public health because the screwworms can also affect people,” said Escobar.
Earlier this summer, the USDA confirmed that the new world screwworm fly reached south Texas, threatening the livestock industry for the first time in decades.
Screwworm-related losses exceeded $200 million annually in the 1950s, the equivalent of roughly $1.8 billion today, before eradication efforts succeeded.
According to Escobar, mitigation measures include mandatory physical inspections and anti-parasitic treatments for cattle at southern border ports, as well as stricter movement requirements for animals entering Texas.
As part of the project, Virginia Tech will expand collaborations with Texas A&M, North Carolina State University, the University of Kansas in the United States, Universidad de San Carlos, and Universidad del Valle in Guatemala.
“Rather than addressing one aspect of screwworm control, this project creates a complete decision-support framework that connects surveillance, genetics, producer behavior, and predictive modeling,” Escobar said.
Luis Escobar is an associate professor in the College of Natural Resources and Environment at Virginia Tech. He is a member of the Pandemic Prediction and Prevention Destination Area, the Invasive Species Collaborative, and the Fralin Life Sciences Institute’s Center for Zoonotic and Arthropod- borne Pathogens and Global Change Center.
His research focuses on biogeography, ecology, and evolution of infectious diseases across landscapes.

articles.title_orig: USA Cycling Announces the 2026 UCI Para Cycling Track World Championships Team
articles.title_zh: USA Cycling Announces the 2026 UCI Para Cycling Track World Championships Team
articles.content_orig:
15 riders are set to compete in Apeldoorn, Netherlands on October 29-November 1, 2026.
The 2026 UCI Para-Cycling Track World Championships will take place October 29-November 1 in Apeldoorn, Netherlands, bringing the world’s best para cycling track athletes together for four days of racing.
Para Cycling track athletes compete across two divisions: Cycle (C), for riders on conventional bicycles with adaptations as needed, and Tandem (B), where visually impaired athletes race alongside a sighted pilot.
USA Cycling will field four tandems in Apeldoorn, including several returning athletes and new pairings.
Branden Walton (Livermore, Calif.) and pilot Ian Anderson (Fort Collins, Colo.) return to the World Championship boards after earning bronze in the Tandem Pursuit at last year’s World Championships in their first international event together. Michael Murphy and pilot Harrison Devine will make their World Championship debut as a tandem after impressing at this year’s National Championships, while Michael Stephens (Colorado Springs, Colo.) and pilot Joe Christiansen (Lyons, Colo.) will take on the sprint events. Current Pan-Am Champion Hannah Chadwick (Arcata, Calif.) will also race the tandem sprint events alongside her new pilot, Hayley Bates (Long Beach, Calif.).
In the C classes, Allison Jones (Colorado Springs, Colo.), Shawn Morelli (Meadville, Penn.), and Katie Walker (Chula Vista, Calif.) will all return to the World Championship boards. Morelli enters the competition as the reigning bronze medalist in the WC4 Scratch Race, and Jones is coming off her bronze medal in the 2026 UCI Para-Cycling Road World Championships Time Trial.
On the men’s side, four MC4 riders will represent the U.S., including Ryan Jastrab (Apple Valley, Calif.), Jason Macom ( Colorado Springs, Colo.), John Terrell (Colorado Springs, Colo.), and Brady Hout (Ronan, Mont.), who will make his World Championship debut.
“We’re really excited to take this team to Apeldoorn for the World Championships,” said Chris Furber, Senior Director of Para Cycling. “Last year we came away with two medals, and our ambition is to build on that performance. For us, it’s about adding value to performance, with every member of the team focused on how they can make a positive contribution to each athlete’s performance. Just as importantly, this is a learning environment. With only three major track events from here until the LA 2028 Games, we have limited opportunities to prepare our athletes at this level. We need to learn and improve quickly to make every opportunity count.”
USA Cycling will be supported in Apeldoorn by coaches Ben Sharp, a longtime Olympic and Paralympic medalist coach, and Pete Mitchell, a seven-time World Champion tandem pilot for Team GB.

articles.title_orig: PWHL Coaches And Managers Continue To Take Over The World
articles.title_zh: PWHL Coaches And Managers Continue To Take Over The World
articles.content_orig:
The PWHL features the world's best women's hockey players. The league has drawn on-ice talent from across the globe into what now stands as a 12-team league.
While the league's impact has been felt on the ice, it's also being felt off the ice as leagues across the globe look to synchronize rules such as body checking to mimic and prepare athletes for the PWHL. The league also forced a shift in the international calendar moving the IIHF women's World Championships to November each year, and last year competing in the Olympics for the first time.
Kori Cheverie - Photo @ Ellen Bond
The league however, has had a notable impact internationally in coaching and management as well. Originally, it was a small group. Gina Kingsbury and Troy Ryan were the general manager and head coach for Team Canada, a staff which also included PWHL coaches like Kori Cheverie, Caroline Ouellette, and Brad Kirkwood. Czechia was also coached by Ottawa Charge head coach Carla MacLeod.
This offseason however, there's been a shuffle, and the connections between the PWHL and international competition have continued to deepen.
This week, that included the addition of Delaney Collins, head coach for Hungary, who was added as an assistant coach with the Vancouver Goldeneyes .
Earlier in the offseason, Canada's coaching staff got a makeover with Kingsbury and Ryan being replaced by a new group of PWHL ties. It's a group led by Daniele Sauvageau, general manager of the Walter Cup winning Montreal Victoire who will serve as Canada's new GM. Last year Sauvageau served as general manager for Italy leading up to the 2026 Olympics. Given the nature of the role, Sauvageau plans to finish her season in Montreal before stepping away from the PWHL to focus on her role with Hockey Canada.
Daniele Sauvageau discusses guiding Team Canada
Sauvageau named Kori Cheverie the new head coach for Canada , a role she already serves with Montreal, and she'll be joined by Montreal asssitant Caroline Ouellette, who will also be an assistant with Canada. Reigning PWHL Coach of the Year Kris Sparre, who won the award last season while guiding the Boston Fleet, will also take on an assistant coach role with Canada this season while he shifts to serve as new head coach for PWHL Hamilton.
Rounding out Canada's staff are a pair of new assistant general managers who serve as GMs in the PWHL in Mike Hirshfeld (Ottawa Charge) and Manon Rheaume (PWHL Detroit).
While the Toronto Sceptres have yet to announce it, Czechia's women's general manager Tereza Sadilova is reported to be joining the team as their new Director of Hockey Operations.
While Gina Kingsbury will no longer serve as general manager for Canada, she is taking on a new leadership role as the new general manager for Austria . She'll be joined by Melody Davidson who will serve as an advisor, a similar role she holds, along with a scouting role for the Ottawa Charge.
Team USA has only one tie to speak of in American national team assistant coach Josh Sciba, who is set to enter his first season as head coach for PWHL Detroit after serving as an assistant coach with the New York Sirens.
Even past PWHL connections are making their mark globally. With Carla MacLeod stepping away from Czechia, she's being replaced by former Vancouver Goldeneyes head coach Brian Idalski. Conversely, Ulf Lundberg who joined PWHL San Jose as an assistant coach this season was head coach for Sweden at the 2026 Olympics.
The PWHL's global footprint is one that continues to grow on both sides of the boards, with coaches taking their talents global, and players moving to join the league.

articles.title_orig: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.title_zh: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.content_orig:
Twenty years ago, wind, solar and other non-hydro renewables were close to a rounding error. In 2005 they supplied a mere 2.0% of the world’s electricity generation. By 2015 that had risen to 6.8%, and by 2025 it was up to 19.8%. According to the IEA Electricity 2026 outlook, non-hydro renewables will supply around 21.8% of global electricity in 2026, edging past natural gas (21.6%) to become the second-largest source of power after coal. 1
That is a remarkable pace of growth from an industry that barely existed two decades ago. But not everyone is impressed; many commenters on social media have responded to these figures by pointing out that despite the growth of renewables, fossil fuel generation continues to grow as well. They aren’t wrong; global coal generation set a record in 2024. Gas generation reached a new high in 2025.
Their point is that clean energy isn’t replacing fossil fuels at all. It’s simply being piled on top of them to feed an ever-growing appetite for electricity, making this an “energy addition” rather than an energy transition. Global fossil electricity generation around 50% higher today than it was in 2005. Coal generation rose by 3,300 TWh and gas by 3,200 TWh. The world burns more coal for power now than it did when wind and solar started taking off.
This argument has been made in the past both by skeptics of growth and by energy systems modelers. The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz argues in More and More and More (2024) that “far from the industrial era passing through a series of transformations, each new phase has in practice remained almost wholly entangled with the previous one.” Coal mining created a huge new demand for timber for pit props, while the oil age ran on steel made with coal. Vaclav Smil has made the same point about today’s clean energy boom more bluntly: ”We use more fossil fuels today than at any time in history… Renewables are not replacing fossil fuels; are joining them.”
The problem with the “addition” argument is that it compares the world today with the world in 2005, rather than with the world as it would have been without clean energy. Electricity demand has not grown because wind turbines and solar panels were built. It has grown because of what the IEA describes as “rising consumption from industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centers”. Demand growth is located overwhelmingly in emerging and developing economies, which accounted for about 80% of global demand growth in 2025 and an average of 95% over the past decade.
Global electricity demand rose by 75% (13,600 TWh) between 2005 and 2025. That demand had to be met by something. Wind and solar supplied 5,400 TWh of new demand, hydro 1,500 TWh, bioenergy and other renewables 530 TWh, nuclear 85 TWh, and fossil fuels the remaining 6,100 TWh. But over the past decade the balance has shifted sharply toward clean energy. Since 2015, wind and solar supplied 57% of demand growth, compared with 29% for fossil fuels. And in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 , “wind and solar grew by 841 TWh, meeting 99% of global electricity demand growth”.
A 2024 study by Brantley Liddle found that “intermittent renewables (solar and wind) have unitary displacement effect.” In other words, each unit of wind and solar power displaced about one unit of coal and oil generation. Fossil generation has kept rising in many years because demand has grown faster than clean energy could be added. That is very different from clean energy failing to displace anything.
And electricity demand will continue to rapidly grow, particularly if we succeed in reducing global emissions by electrifying sectors of the economy that currently burn fossil fuels. Most scenarios where we reach net zero emissions involve a doubling or tripling of electricity generation.
So if we want to assess the real world emissions impact of wind and solar buildout over the past 20 years, the right question to ask is not “did fossil use go down?” but rather “how much higher would it have been?”
To answer this, I built a counterfactual for the global power sector in which wind and solar (and geothermal, which is less than 2% of the total) stopped growing in 2005. In every separate country, their generation is held at 2005 levels, while electricity demand, nuclear, hydro and bioenergy follow their real-world paths. 2 The missing clean generation has to come from somewhere, and in this counterfactual it comes from fossil fuels.
The key choice is which fossil fuels are used to fill in the gap. A wind farm in China or India displaces coal, while one in Texas or the UK mostly displaces gas. So rather than assuming a single global fossil mix, the analysis fills each country’s gap with that country’s own coal, gas and oil mix in each year, using data for about 200 countries from Ember . This keeps real-world coal-to-gas switching like what occurred during the US shale gas boom in place, rather than crediting it to renewables. 3
Without wind and solar growth since 2005, global power-sector CO2 emissions in 2025 would have been 28% higher, at 16.9 billion tonnes rather than 13.2 billion. This adds up to 3.7 billion tonnes avoided in 2025, which is about three-quarters of the total CO2 US emissions that year (or roughly 1.5x EU emissions).
Between 2006 and 2025, wind and solar avoided about 23 billion tonnes of CO2. The biggest assumption I’ve made is what fossil fuel fills in the gap: if every missing kilowatt-hour had come from gas, avoided emissions would be 15 billion tonnes, while if it was all coal it would have been 30 billion.
This lines up almost exactly with Ember’s own estimate. Using a simpler method (and a 2000 baseline rather than 2005 baseline), Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 found that “had wind and solar not grown since 2000, fossil generation would have been 30% higher in 2025, and emissions 28% higher.”
While its true that global electricity emissions have yet to clearly peak, it may well be imminent; emissions went down in 2025 and may be on track to decline in 2026 as well, though rapid increases in demand from vehicle electrification and data centers have made this a bit more challenging. 4 But there are many countries in which electricity emissions have already peaked and declined substantially, and where clean energy has played a key role in those declines.
Globally, clean energy has not yet led to fossil fuel use peaking in the electricity sector. In 2025, fossil generation was essentially flat (down ~0.3%). But that global total hides a lot of country-level variability. In many wealthier economies, where demand has grown more slowly, clean energy has driven real emissions reductions (even when accounting for the outsourcing of some industrial production).
Between 2005 and 2025, power-sector CO2 emissions fell by 75% in the UK, 55% in the European Union and 37% in the United States.
The reasons why differ from place to place:
In the EU, wind and solar account for about 85% of the decline (512 of 601 million tonnes), even though falling nuclear output pushed emissions up by about 100 million tonnes.
In the UK, the decline had three main drivers: wind and solar (56 million tonnes), lower domestic generation (58 million tonnes, partly because the UK now imports more power), and the near-elimination of coal, which went from 45% of UK fossil generation to effectively zero (36 million tonnes).
In the US, switching from coal to cheaper natural gas cut emissions by 682 million tonnes, slightly more than wind and solar (606 million tonnes), while a 12% rise in electricity use added 352 million tonnes. Coal’s share of US fossil generation fell from 69% to 29%.
Without wind and solar growth, EU power emissions would have fallen by only about 16% since 2005 rather than 55%, US emissions by about 17% rather than 37%, and UK emissions by about 53% rather than 75%. Puerto Rican artist Jay Wheeler has announced the “La Voz Favorita” World Tour, produced by Dynamic Records in partnership with AUL Worldwide and UTA, taking the urban music star to major venues across Europe, the United States and Latin America beginning December 2026.
Presale begins Wednesday, Oct. 7 at 11:00 a.m. local time, while the general onsale starts Friday, October 9 at 11:00 a.m. local time.
“La Voz Favorita” Tour 2026 will kick off in Spain on December 4, 2026, in Tenerife, followed by stops in Gran Canaria, Málaga, Valencia, Bilbao, Madrid and Barcelona, where the European leg will conclude on Dec. 19 with a performance at Palau Sant Jordi.
In March 2027, Wheeler will bring the tour to the United States, with performances in major markets and venues including MGM Music Hall in Boston, Kaseya Center in Miami, Coca Cola Roxy in Atlanta, Fillmore in Denver, YouTube Theater in Los Angeles and many others, with Latin America dates in April and June at markets including Quito, Lima, Tegucigalpa, Guatemala City, Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Panama City, San José, Bogotá and Santo Domingo.
“This La Voz Favorita tour is going to be very special. Seeing and hearing all my fans sing along to my songs is one of the most beautiful parts of this career, and I feel truly blessed to have the opportunity to experience it all over again,” said Jay Wheeler.
The tour marks a new chapter in Wheeler’s career, according to the announcement, with Wheeler’s new album seeing multiple hits including “De Lejitos,” which reached No. 1 on Billboard Latin Airplay and Latin Rhythm Airplay, while also reaching No. 7 on Billboard Hot Latin Songs, where it remained in the Top 10 for 11 consecutive weeks.
The booking agency for the tour is AUL Worldwide, with offices in Miami, Los Angeles, Bogotá and Mexico City, led by founder and CEO Adrian Urgelles, who has overseen Jay’s touring alongside with Dynamic Records since 2023.

articles.title_zh: Yemeni government forces advance to Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s deputy defense minister said government forces have taken “full control” of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Perim Island, according to a local news outlet citing Al-Arabiya TV.
“We have taken full control of Bab al-Mandab and Mayun Island, and the military operation is ongoing,” the Yemeni official was quoted as saying.
The reported claim marks a major potential development in the Iran war, as Bab al-Mandeb is a critical maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Vice President JD Vance said the U.S. is reviewing flight security procedures after the FlyDubai terrorist attack, warning that people who pose flight risks should not be allowed “behind the wheel of an airplane.”
“Any time you have any person coming from outside the United States, you've got to be extra careful that that person is actually, one, a good human being, is going to contribute to American society,” Vance told reporters on the tarmac before a trip to Alaska.
Vance said the lesson of the 9/11 attacks was that “we brought a lot of people into the United States of America who shouldn't have been here and certainly shouldn't have been flying planes.”
“We're certainly looking at our procedures within the United States to make sure that people who are obviously flight risks are not getting behind the wheel of an airplane,” Vance said.
Vance said he felt “good” about what is happening in the U.S. regarding potential Iran involvement, but deferred to CIA Director John Ratcliffe and intelligence officials, adding that he had not seen “anything conclusive.”
Vice President JD Vance said the U.S. is taking extreme precautions at overseas military installations after suspected terrorist activity near a British base where U.S. bombers had been stationed.
Asked about suspected Iranian involvement in the U.K. incident, Vance said officials are being “as careful as we possibly can be” and described the U.S. bomber withdrawal as a move made out of caution to protect American forces.
“What you saw there is the Secretary of War, out of an abundance of caution, trying to protect our guys,” Vance said.
“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they're trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as wel. So we are being extremely cautious.”
President Donald Trump is preparing to ease limits on the use of a tax-exempt variety of diesel fuel as the Iran war strains global fuel supplies, Bloomberg News reported Monday.
The plan targets so-called dyed red diesel, although Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
The reported move comes as oil executives warn refined fuel supplies remain tight , with Kuwait Petroleum Corporation estimating about 6 million barrels per day of refined products are missing from the market and Saudi Aramco warning it could take up to two years to replenish global stockpiles.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Yemeni government forces have reportedly taken control of Mocha, a port city west of Taiz, from Houthi terrorist militias, according to a local news outlet citing a public post on X.
“The Armed Forces have taken control of the city of Mokha, west of Taiz, from the Houthi terrorist militias,” the post read.
The reported advance comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces press a broader offensive against the Iran-aligned Houthis, including near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait , a critical Red Sea shipping chokepoint.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday the United States intends to honor its defense and security agreement with Saudi Arabia as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces battle to retake territory from the Iran-backed Houthis near a key Red Sea shipping route.
“The United States has a defense and security agreement with Saudi Arabia , and we intend to live by it: I won't discuss details further than that,” Rubio told reporters Monday.
"As far as our view of it, why I think it's the Saudis and the Yemeni forces clearly are not in favor of a ruthless control in that territory close to the to the strait there and its territory that was gained as a result of a Houthi offensive. And this is the counter to what we expect that that would happen. And that's what's happened.
"So obviously the Saudis have come under attack and, and can see the threat that that poses and they have a right to defend themselves. And obviously, the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. still has confidence in the security of all its bases after an incident at a British air base used by American forces.
Rubio said the British “couldn’t be more cooperative” in responding to the incident.His comments came after U.S. B-1 bombers were removed from RAF Fairford, a key U.S. air base in the U.K., following arrests tied to a suspected Iran-backed plot near the facility.
"It's not unusual to see rotations happen and move into the different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployment, people changing out and people coming in, new planes coming in, old planes going out," Rubio told reporters Monday. "So crews are changing all the time. You guys are just really focused on that now because you still have confidence in British security at the base.
"But we have confidence in the security of all of our bases, because all of our bases are theoretically could be threatened at any moment. and that's why there's so much security built around them.
"And, with the Brits, we work very closely for a very long time, including on this investigation. And they couldn't be more cooperative."
An LPG tanker transiting inbound into the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile Sunday, according to a warning from United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
The reported strike marks another escalation near the critical oil and gas chokepoint , where merchant vessels have faced mounting threats during the Iran war.
The incident follows a string of recent tanker attacks and warnings in and around Hormuz, including a separate UKMTO report that a tanker was hailed by Iran’s IRGC and ordered to turn back or risk being targeted.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog warns of escalating regional threats as Iran increases attacks near the Strait of Hormuz.
Herzog told Fox News' " America's Newsroom " on Monday hailed the importance of military readiness and U.S. support.
The discussion comes as Israel honors victims of the Oct. 7 terror attacks, marking three years since the tragic events.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell nearly 1.7% to $89.61 a barrel Monday after Middle East crude exports increased and G7 nations pledged to release more emergency supplies.
WTI dropped below $90, while global Brent crude slipped 0.4% to $101.82 a barrel as markets weighed fresh supply against continuing disruption fears from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves and pledged to avoid energy export restrictions.
The move comes as Middle Eastern crude exports rose above pre-war levels in four of the final seven days of September, despite attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
Still, PVM Oil Associate analyst Tamas Varga warned that renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis would keep attacks on energy infrastructure and vessels in focus, maintaining an elevated geopolitical risk premium .

U.S. News & World Report and The Princeton Review have ranked the University of Lynchburg among the nation’s best colleges and universities.
In its 2027 edition of “Best Colleges,” U.S. News ranked Lynchburg 332nd among National Universities and 154th in the Top Private Schools category. Lynchburg’s nursing program ranked 557th, and the University ranked 329th in Top Performers on Social Mobility, which recognizes schools that “performed best in … Pell Grant graduation rates and Pell Grant graduation rate performance.”
Lynchburg also is listed in “The Best 392 Colleges: 2027 Edition,” published by The Princeton Review. Lynchburg also was ranked among The Princeton Review’s “Best Mid-Atlantic” colleges and universities.
“These recognitions demonstrate the strength of the University of Lynchburg community,” said Dr. Sally Selden, the University’s president. “We offer an education grounded in academic excellence, personal connection, and student engagement.
“Our students thrive because they are supported by faculty and staff who are deeply committed to their success, both in and out of the classroom. I’m proud of the work happening across our campus and grateful that our student experience is being recognized nationally.”
According to U.S. News, its “Best Colleges” are “ranked according to their performance across widely accepted indicators of excellence.” You can read more about the methodology U.S. News uses to compile its rankings here .
The Princeton Review stated that its 2027 list “brings together survey results from over 172,000 students across the country to find out what they love the most about these schools in everything from financial aid and career services to sustainability and quality of life.”
Those surveyed about the University of Lynchburg described its students as “friendly and willing to work together and help each other out” and said the University was “beginning to have more cultural diversity.” Its reputation for “Southern hospitality” was also noted.
One student put it this way: “Everyone is very helping. If someone is not able to help you with a homework question or a project, then they will find you someone who can. It does feel like one giant family here.”

articles.title_orig: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.title_zh: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.content_orig:
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.
However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl who it said was near the teenager as saying he did not pick up the grenade.
"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.
When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.
"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."
According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."

articles.title_zh: United Methodist elected federation world vice president
articles.content_orig:
Patricia Petudzai Mapani, 61, a United Methodist from Harare, was elected world vice president of the World Federation of Methodist and Uniting Church Women on Aug. 27 at the organization’s world assembly in Auckland, New Zealand.
The Chisipiti United Methodist Church member has held several leadership positions in the organization over the past two decades.
She served as president of the South and East Africa Area 2022-2026 and vice president of the area 2016-2022. Before that, Mapani was The United Methodist Church in Zimbabwe’s unit coordinator for eight years.
“I am driven by passion to support, encourage, empower women and girls and being the voice of the voiceless,” she told UM News.
“It was a very tight election and I felt most humbled to have been chosen. I am still in awe. I am very thankful to the Almighty God for the opportunity to serve at a global level,” Mapani said.
As area president she expanded the area from eight to 18 units, increased attendance at seminars and established the Africa University Scholarship Fund, which enables disadvantaged young women to pursue higher education. She also introduced monthly dawn prayer meetings that are held virtually and have strengthened spiritual life of members in the area.
Her vision is to faithfully strengthen the federation by supporting the world president, coordinating materials and United Nations programs, promoting prayer, women’s empowerment and sustainable partnerships, and safeguarding and sustaining Christ’s transforming mission through hope, unity and love.

articles.title_orig: Dennis Hastert, Powerful Politician Disgraced by Child Sexual Abuse, Dies
articles.title_zh: Dennis Hastert, Powerful Politician Disgraced by Child Sexual Abuse, Dies
articles.content_orig:
He was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars.
CHICAGO -- Dennis Hastert, whose congressional legacy as the longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.
Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007 and spent more than a year in prison later in life, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.
When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.
In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP’s poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job in 1999, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton’s impeachment trial.
After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda.
In 2015 he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors said Hastert’s alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in Yorkville, a small town west of Chicago.
Prosecutors said Hastert sexually abused at least four team members during his coaching career, which lasted from 1965 to 1981.
The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.
Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.
Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.
At the sentencing hearing, where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a “serial child molester.”
In a statement, Hastert said he was “deeply ashamed” and admitted that he "mistreated” some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.
When he became House speaker, Hastert was aware of the pitfalls of holding the powerful position.
"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. “But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground.”
As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert’s aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.
"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," Hastert wrote in a 2004 memoir.
Hastert’s journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.
In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.
Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.
In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.
Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.
He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.
Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master’s in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.
In 2007, Wheaton named its new public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert’s indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.
Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family's feed business.
Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.
Tarm and McCann are former Associated Press reporters. Associated Press reporter Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: World Food Program USA and Suzanne Collins Call on Hunger Games Fans to Help Deliver One Million Meals to Families Facing Hunger Around the World
articles.title_zh: World Food Program USA and Suzanne Collins Call on Hunger Games Fans to Help Deliver One Million Meals to Families Facing Hunger Around the World
articles.content_orig:
The global fan challenge celebrates the upcoming release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping by Lionsgate, based on Suzanne Collins' bestselling novel, and offers multiple ways to help create a world without hunger
WASHINGTON , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ahead of the theatrical release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on November 20, 2026 , World Food Program USA, Suzanne Collins, and Lionsgate today launched a global fan challenge to deliver one million meals to families facing hunger around the world. This challenge is part of a robust campaign to raise awareness and critical funds for global hunger during the end-of-year giving season. Fans can use their generosity, creativity, and voices to help build a hunger-free world by taking action at wfpusa.org/HungerGamesMovie .
"Freedom from hunger is a basic human right, which is why my family has long supported World Food Program USA," said Suzanne Collins. "Please join us in spreading the word about the need to secure adequate nutrition for our neighbors around the world."
Every fan action supports the mission of the World Food Programme (WFP), which delivers food and hope to families across the globe when they need it most. To get started, fans can visit wfpusa.org/HungerGamesMovie to learn more and take the following actions powered by the Zero Hunger Generation, World Food Program USA's youth movement for students and young professionals to help end world hunger.
Fans can do even more with the Zero Hunger Generation . For a limited time, Zero Hunger Generation members can join a Hunger Games book club and post a reaction to the film upon its release to earn special The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping badges and certificates. Through the Zero Hunger Generation program, World Food Program USA is mobilizing a community of young people around hunger relief with educational, service-oriented, and career-building activities.
Today, over 260 million people globally experience severe hunger. In the hardest-to-reach places on Earth, WFP is there saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability, and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters, and the impact of extreme weather.
To reach fans across the globe, World Food Program USA will deploy a campaign alongside Lionsgate, WFP, and ShareTheMeal that cuts across social media, digital advertising, email, SMS, a U.S. TV public service announcement, and that will feature special messages from cast members calling on fans to get involved. World Food Program USA's goal is to help fans learn how small actions can make a big impact and inspire the next generation of hunger relief advocates.
"We are grateful to our generous partners Suzanne Collins and Charles Pryor, and Lionsgate, for helping us engage Hunger Games fans in the movement to end global hunger," said Barron Segar, President and CEO of World Food Program USA. "Hunger is one of the world's most urgent crises, but it is also solvable. By donating, sharing a message of hope, or lending their voice, this generation of fans can become part of the solution."
*Fans ages 18+ can donate at wfpusa.org/HungerGamesMovie.
About World Food Program USA:
World Food Program USA, a 501(c)(3) organization based in Washington, D.C., proudly supports the mission of the World Food Programme by mobilizing American policymakers, businesses and individuals to advance the global movement to end hunger. To learn more, visit wfpusa.org/mission-history .
About the World Food Programme:

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins
articles.content_orig:
Ex-lawyer for woman Tennessee attempted to execute says defense filings said she was at risk for ‘exactly what happened’
A former lawyer for Christa Pike says he was not surprised that Tennessee botched its attempt to execute her because attorneys had warned that problems accessing her veins could make the procedure dangerous and potentially cruel.
James Crowson, who represented Pike during part of her post-conviction appeals, said he had followed the case from afar before the failed execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on 30 September.
“Well, I can’t say I’m surprised,” said Crowson, who represented Pike while working for the Tennessee Post-Conviction Defender. “I knew that there were a number of defense filings saying that she had compromised veins, and that was going to be a difficult and perhaps cruel procedure for her because it was going to put her at risk for exactly what happened.”
Pike, 50, on Sunday remained hospitalized and on a machine helping her breathe after Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that failed to kill her, as far as an attorney now representing her knew, the lawyer said on the CNN program State of the Union.
“She’s still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill – we don’t really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days,” Stephen Ferrell, an assistant federal defender, said to CNN host Jake Tapper.
Ferrell told Tapper that he had not been able to personally see Pike, but “this is the extent of what we know”.
Pike’s attorneys allege improperly placed intravenous lines allowed the drug with which she was injected to enter tissue rather than her bloodstream, leaving both arms severely injured.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that it followed every step of the state’s lawful execution protocol. And the department said the protocol did not permit additional procedures after the steps carried out on Wednesday.
Crowson said the accounts that officials followed the written protocol and that the execution was badly mishandled are not necessarily contradictory.
“The state comes up with a protocol and, typically, states that are inclined to impose the death penalty don’t really include medicine or science in the discussions when they’re coming up with these protocols,” he said.
Crowson said the reported injuries appeared consistent with the concerns raised before the execution, citing the theory that the drug entered surrounding tissue instead of circulating properly through Pike’s bloodstream.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps. Pike was 18 at the time. Her then boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 and was ineligible for the death penalty. He received a sentence of life imprisonment.
That gap in punishment based on a small age difference remains significant to Crowson. He said it illustrates what he views as the capricious nature of capital punishment.
“She’s a few months older than the young man that was engaged in the same conduct, and she’s been fighting for her life now for 32 years,” Crowson said. “He’s still in prison, but hasn’t been subjected to the death penalty.”
He said the age of 18 that was decisive for Pike “just seems like an arbitrary number”.
Crowson represented Pike during a stage of her post-conviction case about 16 years earlier and said he visited her “dozens of times” on death row. He said he last spoke with her in 2009.
He described Pike at the time as “very superficially charming” and attentive to people around her. But he said the person he knew bore little resemblance to the teenager whose crime sent her to death row.
“I never saw the Christa that committed those crimes that put her in prison,” Crowson said. “That person exists, obviously.”
The core of the post-conviction appeal, he said, was ineffective assistance of counsel. His team argued that Pike’s original attorneys failed to adequately present evidence about her mental illness, brain damage and history of severe childhood abuse during the sentencing phase.
Pike ultimately exhausted her appeals without ever getting relief, despite her attorneys’ offering evidence of being diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Crowson more recently said “there was a lot that was left out” at the time of Pike’s conviction.
“Would it have made a difference? I don’t know. There are a lot of people who feel very strongly, and her crime was grisly and horrifying.”
What happens next depends on whether Pike ultimately survives the botched execution – and, if she does, the extent of any lasting injuries.
Crowson said he expects intense pressure on Bill Lee, Tennessee’s governor, to commute Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment if she recovers. If she suffered serious neurological damage, he said, questions about her competency would become central to any attempt by Tennessee to execute her again.
The fallout of the botched execution widened on Saturday when Lee announced Frank Strada, the Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner, would resign later in October. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the remainder of the year.
Strada’s resignation was a predictable consequence of a botched execution now under national scrutiny, according to Crowson, who said: “Whenever you have a disaster like this, there’s going to be some fallout.”
Furthermore, Pike’s was at least the fifth execution Strada had botched since 2022 in Tennessee as well as Arizona, where he previously worked, according to death penalty lawyers.
Crowson said he hopes that Pike’s case results in the government taking a closer look at the death penalty as a functional legal punishment. He said there is a clear pattern between people who are sentenced to death and their history of trauma and mental illness not being accounted for during trial and sentencing.
“I think we as a nation have a strange relationship with mental illness,” he said. “It’s just so often discounted and mocked. It’s unfortunate.”

articles.title_orig: Chicago is the world’s most climate-resilient city. Loyola helped it get there
articles.title_zh: Chicago is the world’s most climate-resilient city. Loyola helped it get there
articles.content_orig:
Chicago topped the list of the world’s most climate-resilient cities, as evaluated by AlphaGeo, a Singapore-based company that ranked 72 of the world’s largest cities based on their exposure to climate risks and ability to reduce adverse impacts from extreme weather events.
“The good news is they call us out and highlight what we have here in Chicago, which is plentiful, clean water and relatively good air quality,” says Aaron Durnbaugh, director of sustainability at Loyola University Chicago. “Although we’re seeing more extreme weather in Chicago, it’s not what folks deal with on the coasts with hurricanes and typhoons or in heavily wooded landscapes prone to wildfires.”
Durnbaugh, a former deputy commissioner in the City of Chicago’s Department of the Environment and one of the chief architects of its pioneering 2008 Climate Action Plan , says Chicago’s privileged geographical location only tells part of the story. The city’s decades-long focus on climate adaptation planning has paid off in infrastructure upgrades, power grid diversification, and emergency response systems that have helped Chicago brace itself for the hostile effects of shifting climate patterns.
Two measures, in particular, stand out.
—
                                    Gilbert Michaud, assistant professor of environmental policy in the School of Environmental Sustainability
Following a heat wave in 1995 that led to the deaths of more than 700 Chicagoans, many of them older adults and people of color, the city invested in new cooling centers, launched wellness checks for at-risk residents, and fortified its power grid to prevent the kind of rolling brownouts that left tens of thousands of residents without power and air conditioning for days during the heat wave.
The city also bolstered its stormwater management infrastructure, widening piping conduits in its combined sewer system, leveraging plant-based infrastructure to absorb rainwater, and partnering with the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago to advance the development of the Deep Tunnel, a 110-mile-long infrastructure system begun in the 1970s and still underway that conveys water to reservoirs and treatment plants through massive underground tunnels.
“We’ve done a lot of things here in our region to improve our infrastructure, including our social infrastructure,” Durnbaugh said. “We’ve created cooling centers. We’ve created social service and public health programs that make sure that people are safe. At the same time, we’ve invested a lot in the hardening of our grid, so that electricity is available even under the most extreme or peak conditions.”
If the recognition comes as welcome news for the city, it is also an auspicious sign for Loyola, whose climate adaptation vision is guided by the Office of Sustainability and the School of Environmental Sustainability and closely aligned with Loyola’s Jesuit mission and commitment to integral ecology.
Under the leadership of Durnbaugh and others, Loyola’s 2015-2025 Climate Action Plan, A Just Future , positioned it to become the first university in the Chicago area to achieve carbon neutrality for its primary energy use. The University’s progress toward net-zero emissions has fulfilled several recent milestones, including a commitment to 100 percent renewable electricity ; $150 million invested in high-performing buildings and the long-term Campus Plan ; the growth of SES; and the inclusion of sustainability in the University’s core undergraduate curriculum.
“Both the city and Loyola have recent climate action plans,” says Gilbert Michaud, an assistant professor of environmental policy in the School of Environmental Sustainability. “What I really appreciate is that we’re actually taking tangible steps to achieve them. One of the things you see with these roadmaps is the real rubber hits the road, in terms of implementation. And that’s what gets me excited about Loyola. We’re walking the walk, we’re achieving our targets, and the city is too.”
Durnbaugh cites several efforts that have helped Loyola draw national attention for its climate resiliency efforts—and they go well beyond decarbonization. In the 1990s, when erosion threatened the stability of high-rises south of campus, Loyola built a sea wall along Lake Michigan to fortify the shoreline near Santa Clara Hall, and raised several building foundations to prevent groundwater infiltration.
More recently, Loyola expanded a chiller plant to keep buildings cool in the face of warming temperatures, created text-based emergency alert systems, and implemented an extensive stormwater management system that includes 17 green roofs spanning more than 55,000 square feet , along with rain gardens, semi-permeable walkways, and underground stormwater infiltration vaults. The system diverts an estimated 19 million gallons of water from city sewers annually—enough to connect Chicago to Houston with one-gallon water jugs.
“Our stormwater system is not just taking pressure off of someone down the sewershed from us,” Durnbaugh said. “But also because we’re next to Lake Michigan, we can direct that water where, historically, it used to go, which is back out to Lake Michigan.”
Perhaps the biggest recent energy transition the University has undergone is a 12-year power purchase agreement with Constellation that began on January 1, 2025. Through the fixed-position contract, Loyola has agreed to buy an estimated 81,660 megawatt hours of electricity annually from the Double Black Diamond solar farm, the largest utility-scale solar project east of the Mississippi River.
The solar energy agreement, aligned with Illinois’ target for zero emissions by 2050 under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act , helps Loyola bring more clean, renewable energy onto the PJM regional transmission grid that feeds into ComEd’s local distribution network. Since electricity pricing fluctuates with demand, on hot summer days and cold winter days when electricity is in heavy use, Loyola can earn money back.
“We’re signing a contract to lock in the purchase of renewable energy at a fixed rate,” Michaud said. “Not only is it good from a climate and renewable energy standpoint, but it’s also a hedge against future fuel price increases.”
These efforts, along with students’ active role in biodiesel production, waste diversion, and urban agriculture programs, helped Loyola earn the Platinum rating —the highest possible—from the Association for the Advancement of Sustainability in Higher Education (AASHE) in their Sustainability Tracking, Assessment & Rating System (STARS). Loyola is the first institution in the Midwest to achieve the Platinum designation and joins only 10 other U.S.-based and seven international institutions in receiving the distinction.
Soon, Michaud says, that number could grow as other universities look to pioneering schools like Loyola as models.
“You have other colleges and campuses that are sort of looking at what we’re doing and having conversations with their faculty and staff, and maybe up to the president and board of trustees. Like, should we be doing this too? Should we also invest in solar? Should we also invest in high-performing buildings?”
Durnbaugh and Michaud are, of course, not the only climate resiliency experts at Loyola who have had a hand in shaping Chicago’s climate adaptation strategy.
Karen Weigert, the director of the Baumhart Center for Social Enterprise and Responsibility at the Quinlan School of Business, was the City of Chicago’s first chief sustainability officer, a position created under former mayor Rahm Emanuel. During her tenure, she led the development of the Sustainable Chicago Action Agenda that laid out 24 goals and more than 100 action items to help make the city more livable under changing climate conditions.
Though pleased by the city’s recent designation, she says there is plenty of work still to be done to prepare for growing climate hazards and extend resiliency efforts equitably across Chic

Broadcast Tools Inc., a manufacturer of specialty and “problem-solving” products for broadcast, will be acquired by Inovonics Broadcast.
Founder and President Donald Winget informed his dealers in a letter on Thursday.
“After nearly 40 years in business, I am finally ready to retire,” he wrote.
BTI is based in Sedro Woolley, Wash. Winget wrote that Inovonics will continue the Broadcast Tools name and product line, moving production to its location in Felton, Calif.
“Ben Barber and his team at Inovonics are fully committed to maintaining the excellence of our products and to nurturing the relationships of trust that have been built with you, our dealers, over these many years.”
BTI products include analog and AES routers, remote controls, satellite channel controllers, analog mixers and DAs, silence monitors and program schedulers.
Winget began in broadcasting as a gofer for the chief engineer of a radio station in Eau Claire, Wis., according to a company history on its website. He served in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam war and later started an engineering contracting business, moving it to the Seattle area in the 1970s. Winget and engineer Lee Hurley created Sentry Systems, an early PC-based automation systems.
Winget founded BTI in 1989 while he was chief engineer at KXRX in Seattle. ( Read a company history .)
Inovonics was founded by Jim Wood and Mark Drake in 1972 to make drop-in, replacement tape recorder electronics assemblies for reel-to-reel machines. The company’s line today includes processors, monitors, RDS products, streaming gear and other specialty broadcast items.

Getting some extra storage space on your Mac could be as easy as deleting Apple’s AI features with a new open-source command line tool called RemoveMacAI . There used to be a single Settings toggle for disabling Apple Intelligence , but that was removed in macOS 27. Now, the models stay on your disk, and the features are split up across different settings panes.
As spotted earlier by MacRumors , the RemoveMacAI developer said in a post on Reddit that the tool essentially does what the old settings toggle did, deleting the models and turning the features off:
You have to find about a dozen settings, and several of them are under Screen Time. Even when everything is off, the foundation models stay on disk, and that’s about 12 GB. I wrote RemoveMacAI to do all of it in one go. It turns off Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension and all the summaries, then it deletes the models and stops macOS from downloading them again.
The developer claims the changes persist across macOS updates, and says Dictation will still work. There’s also a “removemacai revert” command that can turn everything back on and allow the AI models to download again if you change your mind.
The developer says Apple’s AI models take up “about 12GB” of space, but it could be even more than that, as some users pointed out in comments on the developer’s Reddit thread. On my MacBook Air, Apple Intelligence is listed as taking up 35.05GB of space, which I found by going to my storage in the Settings app and clicking the “i” icon beside “macOS.” RemoveMacAI also has a “removemacai status” command that can show the size of each individual AI model on your Mac.
