articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_orig: Switzerland becomes first country to ban fur imports and sales
articles.title_zh: Switzerland becomes first country to ban fur imports and sales
articles.content_orig:
In a historic stand against animal cruelty, Switzerland has become the first country in the world to ban both the import and sale of fur.
Last year, the Swiss Federal Council banned all imports of fur and fur products produced using “methods that involve cruelty to animals. ”
Now, the country has taken the next logical step, banning the sale of fur products within its borders, and thus setting a hugely important example for other countries to follow.
As we highlighted last year, we are still waiting on some final details on the exact meaning of “methods that involve cruelty to animals.” What we do know is that this will be decided by the Swiss authorities, not the fur trade, and we strongly encourage them to ensure it includes all sources of fur production.
Given the recent scientific opinion from the European Food Safety Authority and testimony from veterinary associations around the world, anything less than a full ban on products from animals farmed or trapped for their fur would be a travesty.
That’s because there is no way to humanely raise or kill an animal for their fur.
Switzerland’s move should become a watershed moment to end the fur industry once and for all. It is high time for politicians in other countries to follow the lead.
Our team in the United Kingdom recently welcomed the publication of the Government’s Animal Welfare Committee’s opinion on fur sourcing . It made clear the brutal reality of farming and trapping animals for their fur but recognized that more needs to be done at a political level, stating that “consumer and market forces currently do not and cannot provide sufficient pressure to adequately safeguard animal welfare.”
Now the question becomes what can be done to finally put an end to fur.
It’s increasingly recognized that the factory farming of animals for fur is not only immensely cruel and unnecessary—it’s also a danger to public health.
Fur farms pack animals closely together, making these hellish facilities the perfect place for viruses to spread. Because mink are vulnerable to both human and animal influenza viruses, keeping them in large numbers, in cages closely packed together, allows for the spread of COVID and other viruses to humans or other animals living on or near these facilities. In August, the first outbreak of avian flu (H5N1) on a U.S. mink fur farm underscores the urgent reality of these risks.
The cruelty and danger inherent in the fur industry is widely acknowledged. Now we need to harness political will to create permanent change for animals in this space.
This win for animals is also a reflection of just how weak the international fur industry has become. And it is also a testament to the steadfast work of campaigners on the ground there whose persistence has carried the issue forward, through the many legislative steps necessary for this historic outcome.
In this case, the fur trade had recently pushed hard to integrate its own industry-certification scheme into the process. Thankfully, this effort failed, as such scheme would have undoubtably watered down the effectiveness of banning fur imports and sales.
Meanwhile, in the UK, the FurFreeBritain campaign has the support of more than 200 Members of Parliament and Peers and the UK’s new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, recently stated how he was “proud” of the action a previous Labour Government had taken in 2000 to ban fur farming. We urge him to follow Switzerland and move swiftly to introduce a ban on fur imports and sales. Such an initiative that would be as popular and as groundbreaking as that 2000 fur farming legislation. It would end the current double standard that allows the import of fur from animals from other countries who have been caged and killed in fur farms that would be illegal in the UK.
It is time, too, for the European Commission to publish its long-awaited proposal on the future of fur farming and trade in the European Union.
There is no reason for animals to suffer and die for the fur trade. The public knows it, and the calls for an end to the industry are getting louder. The evidence on animal welfare, public health, environmental damage and economic risk grounds is clear: the future must be fur-free.

articles.title_orig: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
articles.title_zh: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
articles.content_orig:
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its  bombers from the military base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
A No 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".
Speaking on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still has full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities have been very cooperative since the incident.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.
The newspaper wrote that the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.
Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, called the US' decision "prudent".
He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced anymore, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it from all sorts of threats."
It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year .
But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will see the US lose a foothold for the country outside continental Europe.
Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called the US' decision to withdraw its bombers "deeply concerning" and called for the government to set out a plan to ensure the country's military bases are "fit for purpose".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
Residents living close to RAF Fairford told the BBC of their relief at the departure of bombers from the airbase, with one local saying she was "thrilled," citing the noise and feeling "increasingly vulnerable" in recent weeks.
Another villager, who said he has seen bombs being loaded aboard aircraft from his back garden, said he knew something was happening when he saw planes leaving "one, after another, after another" on Sunday.

Global association executive selected to lead WTCA into its next chapter, strengthening Member value and connections across its network across nearly 100 countries and territories
NEW YORK , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- World Trade Centers Association ® (WTCA ® ) — an international trade organization connecting more than 300 World Trade Center ® (WTC ® ) locations across nearly 100 countries and territories — today announced the appointment of Annette Gregg as its first female Chief Executive Officer in the Association's 57-year history.
Gregg joins WTCA as the Association enters a new chapter, following the recent return of its global headquarters to the World Trade Center site in Lower Manhattan after 25 years, signaling an exciting new chapter for the organization, and further advancing its mission of "Connecting Businesses, Globally ." As CEO, Gregg will provide strategic leadership to WTCA and its global staff, working closely with the Board of Directors and Members to advance the Association's strategic and business priorities. She will also serve as a leading public voice for WTCA, focused on strengthening engagement across its Membership, expanding the global network and creating new opportunities for Members to connect businesses, markets and communities through international trade and investment.
"Annette brings the combination of strategic vision, financial acumen and global stakeholder engagement that WTCA needs as we look toward the future," said John E. Drew, Chair of the WTCA Board of Directors. "Throughout her career, she has demonstrated that she knows how to strengthen international organizations by listening to their Members, creating meaningful value and building connections across markets and cultures. With Annette stepping into this new role and WTCA recently establishing its headquarters at One World Trade Center, we are building on a strong legacy while positioning the Association for its next era of global growth and impact."
Gregg brings more than 30 years of leadership experience spanning global associations, private enterprise and the international business events and hospitality sectors. Most recently, she served as CEO of the Society for Incentive Travel Excellence (SITE), where she led a global association of approximately 3,700 members and 27 chapters. Under her leadership, SITE increased topline revenue by 160% in three years through diversified revenue streams while expanding membership by more than 70%. She was also recently named the 2026 Marin Bright Legacy Award Recipient for her work with SITE, and her leadership in meetings and events, and was awarded at the 2026 Smart Women in Meetings Awards Gala.
Previously, Gregg served as Chief Revenue Officer for Meeting Professionals International (MPI), where she was responsible for approximately 70% of the organization's revenue and helped expand global product distribution across Europe, Asia and Latin America. Her career has consistently centered on building international communities, strengthening stakeholder engagement and translating the reach of global networks into tangible value for their members.
"WTCA has an extraordinary foundation — a trusted global brand and a network of Members with deep connections to businesses and communities across nearly 100 countries and territories," said Annette Gregg, Chief Executive Officer, WTCA. "I see tremendous opportunity to build on that strength — listening to our Members, connecting ideas and opportunities across markets and finding new ways for this network to create meaningful business value. I'm honored to lead WTCA into this next chapter and excited to help strengthen the connections that make international business possible."
Gregg's appointment comes as businesses are navigating an increasingly complex global environment, making trusted relationships, market intelligence and direct connections across borders increasingly important. Through its network, events and programming, WTCA brings together business leaders, economic development organizations and WTC businesses to exchange market intelligence, develop cross-border relationships and identify opportunities for trade and investment.
She assumes her CEO responsibilities effective October 5 and will lead WTCA from its recently established global headquarters at One World Trade Center in New York City, working alongside the Association's headquarters and regional teams serving Members around the world.

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “recovering” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally recovering”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez announces snap election amid housing crisis
articles.title_zh: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez announces snap election amid housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced a snap general election after Parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
Sanchez said on Monday the vote would take place on November 29. “We need to renew people’s support,” he said in a televised address.
“We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in Parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.”
In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.
The government said more than 70,000 people took part in a housing protest in the capital on Saturday.
For years, housing has been a top concern for Spaniards as current levels fall short of demand. According to real estate website Idealista, average rents have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent.
In his announcement, Sanchez acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of previous campaign promises.
“I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today,” Sanchez said.
But facing the electorate is a risky move for Sanchez. Opinion polls suggest that a coalition led by the conservative People’s Party (PP), with support from the far-right Vox party, is the most likely outcome in the election.
If they win, it will be the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco that a far-right party has entered central government.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged voters to bring his party to power in the election.
“The question I put to voters is whether they want four more years of what we’ve been living through, or whether they want to give change a chance,” he said in a televised address.
If Sanchez loses the election, it will also mark the end of one of Europe’s last left-leaning governments as the far right continues to gain ground across the continent.
Sanchez has stood out worldwide for his strong stance on progressive ideas, from defending the rights of Palestinian people to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on tech oligarchs.
The prime minister, who has never won enough votes to form a majority government, has brought together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, ranging from the far left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms, lasting eight years.

articles.title_orig: Sentence tossed after man killed in 2021 "speaks" in AI video shown in Arizona court
articles.title_zh: Sentence tossed after man killed in 2021 "speaks" in AI video shown in Arizona court
articles.content_orig:
An Arizona man's 10-year manslaughter sentence has been tossed in a case where a video generated by artificial intelligence portrayed the deceased victim addressing a judge before the punishment was imposed.
In a decision released Wednesday, the Arizona Court of Appeals concluded Gabriel Paul Horcasitas must be resentenced in the 2021 shooting death of Christopher Pelkey because the AI video wasn't reliable.
The court found the video crossed the line, saying it didn't reflect actual events and presented statements made in the footage as coming directly from the victim.
"Indeed, rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," the three-judge panel wrote.
Jessica Gattuso, an attorney who represented victims in the case, and Kristen Reller, Horcasitas' lawyer, declined to comment Thursday on the decision.
Reller argued Superior Court Judge Todd Lang violated due process protections by relying on AI evidence. Gattuso and prosecutors told the appeals court that the lower-court judge didn't err, saying the footage was an accurate representation of Pelkey's character.
In what's believed to be a first in U.S. courts, Pelkey's family used AI to create a video of his likeness to give him a voice. Pelkey's sister, Stacey Wales, raised the idea of her brother speaking for himself after struggling to figure out what he would say.
Wales told the BBC last year the family used voice recordings, videos and pictures to re-create him for the AI video.
"To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances," said the AI version of Pelkey in court in 2025. "In another life, we probably could have been friends."
"I believe in forgiveness, and a God who forgives. I always have and I still do," the AI version of Pelkey continued.
Wales expected an appeal on the sentence and was disappointed the AI video was cited as the reason, saying her only goal was to humanize her brother for the judge.
"It feels unfair because there is a convicted murderer sitting in prison that has blankets and walls of protection around their rights. Where are the rights for the victim?" Wales said.
A victim appeals lawyer told the family that using AI again could result in another appeal.
"We will continue to let his voice be heard in whatever allowable medium we can convey that through the court system," Wales said.
The AI-generated victim impact statement was played during a May 2025 sentencing hearing after nine of Pelkey's family members and friends stood before the judge describing how emotionally devastated they were by his killing.
Authorities say Horcasitas, 55, fatally shot Pelkey, 37, during a November 2021 road rage encounter at a stoplight in Chandler, a suburb of Phoenix. Pelkey, who was unarmed, was shot after getting out of his truck and walking toward Horcasitas' vehicle.
Horcasitas was convicted of manslaughter in Pelkey's death and endangerment for a gunshot that struck another vehicle at the intersection during the encounter.
Horcasitas' appellate lawyer argued her client had no meaningful opportunity to rebut material in the AI-generated video.
It's not clear if attorneys or the court were aware in advance that an AI-generated video would be used. But attorneys representing Pelkey's family said in court records that Arizona law does not require victims to disclose statements they plan to make in court to prosecutors, defense attorneys or the judge — and that victims can exercise their rights by speaking before the court or submitting statements that are written or recorded on audio or video.
In a statement Thursday, the Maricopa County Attorney's Office said its prosecutors knew the victim's family would address the court during sentencing but weren't aware of the nature of it.
While the use of AI within the court system is expanding, it's typically been reserved for administrative tasks, legal research and case preparation. In Arizona, it's helped inform the public of rulings in significant cases.
But using AI to generate victim impact statements marks a new tool for sharing information with the court outside the evidentiary phases.
Reller told the appeals court that the video doesn't disclose who wrote the words used by the AI version of Pelkey and wasn't backed up with evidence establishing that its contents accurately reflected Pelkey's views. It also had an "undue emotional weight" and conveyed an authenticity that wouldn't have been there had a family member read the same words aloud, Reller said.
Horcasitas' lawyer contended the judge weighed the statements made in the AI-generated video when deciding on a sentence, but prosecutors argued Lang didn't consider the footage when issuing the punishment.
Shortly before delivering the sentence, the judge commented that he "loved that AI" but didn't say from the bench whether the video factored into his decision. Lang said he felt Pelkey's "obvious forgiveness of Mr. Horcasitas reflects the character I heard about today."
The family's lawyers say the judge was already inundated with relevant information from Pelkey's family and friends before the AI video was played — and that nothing in the video was inflammatory. Horcasitas' attorney didn't object to the AI video.
Gary Marchant, a law professor at Arizona State University, said he understands why Pelkey's family did it. But he warned the use of this technology could open the door to more people trying to introduce AI-generated evidence into courtrooms.
"There's a real concern among the judiciary and among lawyers that deepfake evidence will be increasingly used," he said. "It's easy to create it and anyone can do it on a phone, and it could be incredibly influential because judges and juries, just like all of us, are used to believing what you see."
Marchant pointed to a case in New York, where a man without a lawyer used an AI-generated avatar to argue his case in a lawsuit via video. It took only seconds for the judges to realize that the man addressing them from the video screen didn't exist at all .

articles.title_orig: GM says hybrid vehicles are coming: 'We're not tone deaf to our customers'
articles.title_zh: GM says hybrid vehicles are coming: 'We're not tone deaf to our customers'
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — General Motors plans to introduce hybrid models into its U.S. lineup as sales of the vehicles continue to grow amid inflated gas prices and a pullback in all-electric cars.
Mike Anderson, GM's vice president of propulsion engineering, reconfirmed the automaker's hybrid plans, but declined to discuss timing for such vehicles, which had previously been expected as soon as next year.
"It's fair to say that [hybrids are] part of the plan," Anderson, a 35-year GM veteran, told CNBC during an interview. "We're not tone deaf to our customers. We know what they want and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can."
GM has largely been absent from the hybrid market this decade, instead using its resources to go "all-in" on all-electric vehicles . But amid lackluster EV demand, industry deregulation and increased hybrid popularity, Anderson said the company needs to meet customer demand wherever it may be.
"Our long-term vision is an all-electric future. That's our goal," Anderson said. "That's the end state, but it's going to be a journey that involves technology diversity."
GM CEO Mary Barra in January said the automaker was still studying plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, or PHEVs, for its U.S. lineup as well as traditional hybrids but remained critical of the technologies. She also told Bloomberg later that month that a "handful" of such models were coming but did not give a timeline.
In mid-2024, GM announced plans to introduce PHEVs by 2027. At that time, GM was under pressure to meet stricter federal tailpipe emissions standards that have since been lowered or eliminated by the Trump administration.
AutoForecast Solutions, an automotive data and consulting firm, expects GM to begin offering PHEVs in late 2027 to early 2028 with a 70-mile EV range "throughout its portfolio," according to Casey Selecman, director of powertrain forecasts for the company.
"GM has several PHEVs planned throughout the portfolio from the Equinox to the Silverado but has been very cautious in rolling them out due to fears of customer technology preference changes that have burned them in the past," he said.
Anderson declined to discuss potential products or timing for GM's first new hybrid model.
"You can see, without me saying what our future plans are, where the customers are clamoring for these things and really, really going for them," he said. "We want to meet them where they want things."
Sales of hybrid models in the U.S. have jumped amid dimming EV demand, inflated gas prices and more offerings in the market, which GM has been missing out on.
Cox Automotive reports hybrid vehicle sales from the second quarter of this year increased 23% from a year earlier to represent a record 16.3% of U.S. sales from April through June. That compares with roughly 5.8% of sales for EVs, Cox said.
There are a growing number of hybrid variants being introduced by automakers but, in general, those vehicles combine a traditional gas-powered engine with electric motors and a battery to offer better fuel economy and, in many cases, better performance.
The fastest-growing segments for hybrids in the U.S. are compact crossover/SUV and mid-size vehicles, according to Cox.
"Hybrid vehicles continue to be the clearest growth story in the electrified market," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insights, said during a presentation last week.
There are currently a few types of hybrids available in the U.S. Traditional hybrids, like a Toyota Prius, feature many electrified engine technologies, while PHEVs have a designated all-electric range before using an engine to power the vehicle.
Then there are extended-range electric vehicles, or "series hybrids," that drive like an EV but have an engine that essentially operates like a generator to power electric motors to propel a vehicle.
The combination of two powertrains adds additional complexity and costs, which has been an argument GM has made against hybrids, but it's something many consumers appear willing to pay for as hybrid sales continue to rise.
GM currently offers only one hybrid, a model of its Chevrolet Corvette. The Detroit automaker's last true push into hybrids was the Chevrolet Volt plug-in , which was discontinued in 2019.
GM's crosstown rivals, Ford Motor and Chrysler parent Stellantis , have leaned on suppliers to get hybrid vehicles to market more quickly.
Anderson said GM's strategy "will be a mix" of internal and external technologies based on cost, segment and product.
"We're deliberate because, usually for strategic reasons, we need to control our own destiny. We need to control our own timing," he said. "Or, if it's commodity, go get it. Go get the best price you can."

articles.content_orig:
Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.
The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned , saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.
In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit , warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely].
“I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.”
The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”.
His state last week asked a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails.
Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”.
Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.”
He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together.
“I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.”
Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Musk alleged in court that Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury.
OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk.

The company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation.
The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements.
However, Donald Trump and AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers.
“There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive.
OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next.
His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.

articles.title_orig: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.title_zh: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.content_orig:
A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case.
The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20.
The student recalled rumors that Doe was planning to have a threesome but that it had “gone off the rails,” and she remembers being “really horrified by it.”
“From that night, I think, we just kind of started, like, hearing more,” the student said.
Talk of the alleged sexual assault became widespread on campus after the school issued a crime safety alert about a report of a sexual assault at a fraternity.
“The thing I think we all feel, like, betrayed in regards to is that, like, it wasn’t handled,” she said. “When we got the police report, I think we all assumed it was being, you know, it would be, like, handled properly, yeah, and it was, like, in good hands.”
The student, who discussed details corroborated by documents reviewed by NBC News, said she and a friend initially gave a tip to authorities after the crime alert was issued. Police later called her and asked her to come in and speak with them days after Doe reported the incident to Cornell police on Nov. 8.
The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because “it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl.” Doe’s lawsuit included a screenshot of a Chi Phi Snapchat group message that said there was “free p----” in a room in the frat house where Doe was the night she alleges she was assaulted.
“That was, like, when I kind of internally made the decision. OK, like, I’m taking this all in, and then I’m going to the police tomorrow,” the student said.
She recalled sitting with one or two officers for about half an hour during her interview with police.
“They seemed fairly competent. It seemed like a normal interview process to me,” she said.
She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of that evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she is familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept.
“I guess I assumed that, like, I wasn’t enough,” the student said.
Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday on the student’s account to police. In a video statement Saturday, President Michael I. Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” and said they raise questions about the investigations that were conducted. He said he welcomes an independent review of how the university handled the matter, which will be conducted by an outside law firm.
Police records obtained by NBC News showed that Cornell police spoke to multiple witnesses and fielded anonymous tips about the allegations of a gang rape at the fraternity house — but that the information was not referred to the local prosecutor for review in his deciding whether to bring charges.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NBC News on Friday that the interviews that were flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.” He did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.
Van Houten ultimately determined the allegations did not warrant charges because of a lack of criminality.
Doe’s suit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell and Van Houten’s handling of her allegations. Van Houten has since agreed to reopen his inquiry into Doe’s allegations, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the matter.
The student who spoke with campus police criticized how the department handled the matter. While students believed there was an active investigation into Doe’s claims, people continued going to Chi Phi, including the room at the center of the allegations.
Within Greek life at Cornell, “rumors spread fast,” the student said, and even if you did not know Doe or the men, “you knew someone who did.”
Doe’s lawsuit named Cornell, Chi Phi and the seven fraternity brothers among the defendants. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.
Cornell said in a statement on Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions ” from the university.
According to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation, two of the fraternity members were expelled, and another two were suspected. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and “reflection papers.”
Attorneys for two of the seven men have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the five other men.
Chi Phi’s national fraternity condemned sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in a statement Wednesday. It said that the fraternity members Doe named were kicked out of the organization and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter.
“At every level of Chi Phi, we will take steps like these whenever they are needed to protect the integrity of our fraternity and the safety of our communities,” said Trey Robb, the national fraternity’s interim executive director.
Some of the men faced backlash as talk spread on campus.
Two of the Chi Phi brothers named in the suit were kicked out of their rugby club after the allegations came to light, a former teammate told NBC News.
“We kicked [them] off the team immediately before the school expelled them,” said the teammate, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.
The teammate said he has participated in discussions among a group of current and former rugby players about responding publicly to Doe’s lawsuit.
“As a team, it was important for us to support this victim,” he said. “We are extremely, extremely distraught.”
Cornell Rugby said in a statement that it was “deeply disturbed” by the allegations and that its thoughts were with Doe.
“Players who were known to be connected with the alleged events were permanently removed from the team and alumni network as soon as their affiliation with the incident was established,” it said.
No current members of the team have been affiliated with Chi Phi, the statement said.
As news of the allegations spread, some discussions were supportive of Doe, but others shamed her in conversations, a former member of Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta, told NBC News.
“Some people were sympathizing with Jane Doe, but also, people didn’t know details,” said the former member, who has graduated and requested anonymity out of a concern for privacy.
Another student and former member of Tri Delta told NBC News that she recalled learning about the incident through rumors and described the student body as “really pissed off about it.”
That student said that she was at the same sorority-hosted event the evening of Oct. 19 that Doe attended and which was referred to in her lawsuit but that Doe disappeared during the evening.
A few days later, the student said, Doe said people were spreading rumors about her and she was not sure what to make of it, “and it just seemed like everybody was very confused at the moment.”

articles.title_orig: Athens World War II soldier laid to rest 82 years after death
articles.title_zh: Athens World War II soldier laid to rest 82 years after death
articles.content_orig:
MARIETTA - When Spencer Rutter got the call that after more than eight decades, his uncle's remains had been identified, it didn't take him long to tell the Army where they should end up.
"They belong at Maplewood Cemetery in Glouster, with his parents," Rutter, an 83-year-old Marietta resident, said.
According to the federal Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency, Army Air Forces Sgt. Myron Lee Yaw, an Athens County native, was identified on June 25. He served in the 828th Bombardment Squadron, 485th Bombardment Group, and was killed the day after Christmas in 1944 when the B-24J Liberator on which he was the ball turret gunner was struck by anti-aircraft fire and crashed near the village of Korzonek, Poland.
It's not the homecoming Rutter's grandparents envisioned when their son went overseas to serve in the Army Air Forces. But it's one his mother, Betty Jane Rutter, Yaw's sister, hoped for as the years went on.
A DPAA release says an archaeological survey of the crash site was completed in 2018. Rutter said his mother provided a DNA sample that year. Though she passed away in 2019, her sample eventually led to the positive identification of her brother's remains.
"She knew they had remains, and they probably had his remains," Rutter said. "She would have been beside herself" to know it was confirmed.
Rutter said his mother was extremely close to his Uncle Lee, one of two brothers she lost in the war. And Lee Yaw was a doting uncle who was so excited to have a nephew that Rutter wound up being the mascot on his uncle's plane. An image painted on the plane featured a baby wearing boxing gloves and the name "Butch," his uncle's nickname for him.
"I was the inspiration for nose art on an airplane," Rutter said. "If he had survived the war, I would have been one spoiled nephew."
Yaw's remains were returned to Ohio on Sept. 25 and escorted from the airport in Columbus back to Athens County. A funeral was held on Saturday.

articles.title_orig: TCL’s paperlike OLED phone made me more excited for the iPhone Duo
articles.title_zh: TCL’s paperlike OLED phone made me more excited for the iPhone Duo
articles.content_orig:
More phones should have matte displays.
I’ve spent most of the last couple weeks using an otherwise unexceptional midrange Android phone with one amazing feature: a matte OLED display. That screen is by far the best thing about the TCL P80 Ultra , and weirdly, it’s made me more excited for the iPhone Duo and its matte inner display.
2023’s TCL Nxtpaper 40 first brought matte displays to the company’s phones, after they appeared on tablets in 2021 . Nxtpaper is more than a simple matte finish on a panel: it also includes a paperlike feel and low-power, monochrome modes that create a reasonable facsimile of an E Ink screen. But the matte effect has always been the biggest draw for me.
The P80 Ultra’s screen is special because it’s the first to combine the Nxtpaper tech with an OLED panel. That means it’s the best-looking Nxtpaper screen yet, with deeper blacks, better contrast, and richer colors. Previous models have felt a little visually compromised; this one doesn’t. It also finally enables an always-on display. Always-on displays have been the norm on Android for years, and the fact that TCL’s Nxtpaper phones didn’t have them was a dealbreaker for many.
I’ve used a couple of Nxtpaper phones over the last few years, but usually found the tradeoffs — both across the specs and in the screen itself — never quite made sense. In some respects, that’s still true for the P80 Ultra, which I can’t entirely recommend as a phone in its own right. Performance has been sluggish and stuttering, and while the triple rear camera has decent enough specs on paper, photo quality is distinctly average.
The difference now is that the display feels like all upside. As an OLED, it’s bright and beautiful, with enough color and contrast to suit both scrolling and streaming. But the matte finish keeps it comfortable to look at, even at cranked up brightness or in a dimly lit room, with less flicker and blue light than most other displays. Nxtpaper’s anti-glare effect actually makes this a really excellent phone to use in brighter environments. It looked great under the bright lights of TCL’s IFA tradeshow booth, no mean feat. And the viewing angles are truly excellent, with good visibility even when the phone is almost entirely side-on. That’s without touching on the texture, which is smooth and satiny, so your finger sticks just a little less when swiping. It’s a small thing, but a welcome one.
Because this is a Nxtpaper phone, it goes a little further. A dedicated toggle on the phone’s side triggers one of two more substantial overhauls to the display. Paper Mode washes out the display’s color — or can go fully monochromatic if you prefer — to make it even easier on your eyes, with the option to exclude individual apps so they run as usual. Streaming apps and games are exempted by default. Max Ink Mode is more drastic: it’s strictly monochrome and removes access to most apps and OS features, giving you a power-efficient mode with minimal distractions, turning the P80 Ultra into something between an e-reader and a dumb phone.
Although most other phones are limited to aftermarket matte screen protectors to get anything like the same effect, TCL isn’t the only manufacturer making hardware with a matte display. Huawei has made a string of tablets with what it calls PaperMatte panels , and Lenovo and Xiaomi offer similar screens on select models. Matte screens underpin the painterly effect of Samsung’s Frame TVs (and imitations from rivals including TCL ). And then, of course, there’s Apple’s nano-texture glass.
Apple’s offered this coating as an option on iPad Pro models since 2024 , selling it on the basis that its paperlike qualities are beneficial to anyone using the iPad Pro as a drawing device. It’s now appearing on a phone for the first time in the iPhone Duo, with Apple relying on the anti-glare effect to minimize the visibility of the foldable panel’s crease.
I haven’t had the chance to try the Duo yet, but using the P80 Ultra has made me more excited to. Pairing a matte effect with the Duo’s large inner screen sounds great, and it’s one of the few elements of the Duo that no Android foldable can currently match. My only hesitation is that Apple didn’t make the outer panel matte too — an odd choice given how much it’s emphasized the seamless switch between the two screens — so I worry the transition might be jarring. Given the book-style form factor, Apple will also be missing a trick if it doesn’t create its own e-reader-inspired mode for the Duo to match TCL’s, though the existing grayscale mode might be a decent imitation.
Perhaps what’s most exciting about an iPhone adopting a matte panel is that within the year we’ll probably see Android brands imitate it, something TCL wasn’t able to inspire. We’ve already seen the Duo’s squat form factor appear in handsets from Samsung , Xiaomi , and Huawei , with Motorola teasing its own too . The Duo’s matte layer hasn’t yet sparked its own imitators, but I suspect it’s only a matter of time, especially if it helps hide foldable creases. Not every phone needs to be matte, but I would love more of them to give me the option. Hopefully Apple’s industry influence grants me my wish.

articles.title_orig: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.title_zh: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.content_orig:
When we think of viruses, we often associate them with disease, but many viruses in nature have nothing to do with human illness.
A new study that included Clemson University microbiologist Barbara Campbell suggests that one poorly described group in particular — giant viruses — may be important participants in ecosystems ranging from ocean and freshwater systems to soil.
A collaborative international research team created the largest catalog yet of giant virus genomes. The collection includes 18,727 metagenome-assembled genomes, which are genetic reconstructions made from environmental samples from marine and freshwater systems, soil, rock, thermal springs, plant-associated environments and landfills.
After comparing the genomes, the researchers identified 8,508 species-level representatives, 712 previously unknown genera, 13 new viral families and a proposed new order called Mycodnavirales .
The study, published in the journal Nature Microbiology, provides new clues about the diversity and possible ecological roles of giant viruses.
“We’re interested in what’s going on out there in the environment at the microbial scale,” said Campbell, much of whose research involves the Chesapeake and Delaware bays .  Her group is especially interested in the ecological questions of “Who’s there? What are they doing? What and who are they interacting with?”
The study uses metagenomics to help answer those questions.
Most of the microbes in marine and estuarine environments are difficult to grow in the laboratory, and studying viruses depends on host cells. With metagenomics, scientists collect an environmental sample and sequence all the DNA in it. The genetic material comes from many organisms, and researchers use bioinformatic tools on high-performance computers such as Palmetto to assemble the fragments into larger sequences that can reveal the organisms’ identities.
“It allows us to look to see what’s in the environment without actually having to culture it,” Campbell said.
Despite their name, giant viruses can’t be seen by the human eye.
“They are giant, but giant is relative,” Campbell said. “You still need a microscope to see them.”
Bacteria are huge when compared to viruses. The smallest bacteria are about 0.4 microns in diameter, or one millionth of a meter. Viruses range in size from 0.02 to 0.25 microns. Most viruses are submicroscopic, meaning they are unable to be seen in an ordinary light microscope. They are typically studied with an electron microscope.
But some giant viruses are nearly the size of bacteria, and their genomes can exceed 2.5 million DNA base pairs. They may have hundreds of thousands of genes, including genes related to metabolism and protein production. That genetic complexity gives giant viruses the potential to influence the cells they infect in unusual ways.
Some giant viruses carry genes associated with producing proteins, a process other viruses leave to their hosts. Others contain genes connected to metabolism, stress responses and cell signaling.
“A lot of them have most everything needed to sustain life,” Campbell said.
That doesn’t mean they live independently. They still need host cells to reproduce. But their large genomes may allow them to manipulate host cells in more complicated ways than smaller viruses can.
According to the study, researchers found potential clues about the environmental roles of giant viruses, too. For instance, some groups contained genes associated with processing formaldehyde and breaking down aromatic compounds, including substances that can occur in industrial pollution.
The giant viruses in the study are generally host-specific and are not expected to infect humans. However, their impact could be felt by humans because they may help shape the health of oceans, bays, lakes and soil.
For Campbell, the results reinforce how much scientists still do not know about the smallest life forms in oceans and estuarine waters.
Viruses are part of what scientists call the microbial loop. Many giant viruses infect microscopic organisms such as phytoplankton and protists. When viruses break open their hosts, nutrients inside the cells are released back into the environment where they can be used by other organisms.
In low-nutrient marine and estuarine environments, that recycling can be especially important. Estuarine and marine phytoplankton are essentially single-celled plants that absorb carbon dioxide and produce roughly half the Earth’s oxygen she said.
“So knowing more about what makes them tick, and how they survive and die, is important, and studies like this give us an excellent starting point,” Campbell said.

articles.title_orig: Qalo SL-1 Review: A Barebones Smart Band That's Priced Like A Flagship
articles.title_zh: Qalo SL-1 Review: A Barebones Smart Band That's Priced Like A Flagship
articles.content_orig:
It’s the same price as the Garmin Cirqa.
I've already made my feelings about screenless fitness trackers well known to everyone who'll listen. They're more about signaling to the in-crowd that you're a serious gym goer than a better alternative to a proper smartwatch. Still, that's a big enough market that plenty of companies are jostling for space alongside Whoop (and Fitbit, and Garmin). Take Qalo, a jewelry brand with a side hustle selling smart rings, which is now branching out with its own screenless band. The Qalo SL-1 is a subscription-free band which aggregates all of your vital signs into a single score.
If you're unfamiliar, Qalo sells silicon rings for folks who, for many reasons, can't or won't wear a metal ring. If you work in heavy industry, it's wise to swap your wedding band for something that won't cause you to lose a finger in an accident. They're also a great option for the gym or other physical activities, as well as for folks who experience finger-swelling.
Qalo has launched two generations of rings in the last few years, with some corners of the internet saying they're re-branded hardware from J-Style, a white-label wearables manufacturer. A representative of the company told me that the SL-1 , however, is "built around QALO's own software, data and design."
It's worth understanding that if you own a Qalo smart ring, the SL-1 is complimentary with the rest of its ecosystem. So if you wear a ring during the day, but take it off for the gym, you can strap the band on your wrist or bicep and all of the data will aggregate to the same place.
At $199.95, Qalo is asking for the same sort of money as Garmin wants for its own smart band, the Cirqa . Which means there's an easy benchmark to see if this generic, first-generation hardware is capable of outperforming a wearables specialist with decades of experience.
The Qalo SL-1 is a screenless fitness tracker which looks like someone described a Whoop over the phone. It's a little longer than a Whoop MG but, to my eye, has a more pronounced bend in its chassis, although that didn't seem to affect how it sat on my wrist. Take it out of the box and you'll first notice the silicon strap, which attaches to itself magnetically.
In that initial moment, the idea of a magnetically-attached watch strap looks and sounds like the coolest idea imaginable. It'll take you all of 30 seconds to realize why other watchmakers don't do the same thing with their own products. Because, as elegant as the magnetic strap is, it will get easily dislodged if your sleeve slides along at the wrong angle.
Qalo says the water-resistant band lasts for 12 days on a single charge, and will keep an eye on the usual set of vital signs. That includes activity, sleep, heart rate, SpO2, HRV, stress, temperature and menstrual cycle tracking. It ships with a magnetic USB-C charging cradle which I would describe as heavy for what it is.
Like the devices it's competing with, the SL-1 collects a trove of data about you, but knows it's too much for you to take in. Consequently, it produces a Q Score, a single 1-100 metric telling you how well you're looking after yourself and how much fuel is in your tank. As you can see from the screenshot, the score is joined by three other metrics: Sleep, Movement, and Vitality. The latter aggregates your resting heart rate, resting HRV, blood oxygenation level and skin temperature.
Open the app each morning, and you'll get a pop-up telling you your Q Score for the previous day. Get enough sleep and exercise, and that figure will be high, and if you look after yourself for several days in a row, you'll get a streak encouraging you to keep it going.
Once dismissed, you'll be able to look at the home screen, which provides live updates on Q Score throughout the day. Annoyingly, its conclusions exist in a vacuum, and are written past-tense. Look at this first thing in the morning and you'll be told your score is low because you didn't log a workout and didn't walk enough. It's not a big deal in and of itself, unless you're really sensitive to being demoralized by your fitness wearable. But it's a sign the system does little beyond aggregating the data it's given, ignoring the broader context.
I'm also disappointed at the lack of automatic workout detection, at least for the basics, which should be a standard feature for any fitness band. The fact the SL-1 can't identify when I'm out for a walk and log that separately vexes, especially given the likelihood I'll forget to activate a workout. This omission may be easier to take if you couldn't get a product like Garmin's Cirqa for the same amount of money, which can do this.
Start an activity, and you'll get details on your heart rate zones, maximum and average HR, steps and calories burned. You'll even get your live heart rate and the zone you're in as a live activity on your phone's lock screen. You'll then get a breakdown of your heart rate zones and calories burned at the end of a workout, again much like you'll find on other devices.
One thing I cannot fault the SL-1 for is its battery life, and I suspect it'll make it at least past its 12-day promise. I've worn this thing a full week, and the battery is still reporting a charge level of 59 percent, which is worthy of praise in and of itself.
One of the hard things about testing the Qalo SL-1 was the fact I don't think it did anything well enough to outperform its rivals. There's no single killer feature it offers that would compel me to recommend it over any other screenless fitness tracker out there. Instead, it feels like the unit you'd recommend to someone who simply wanted to dip a toe into this market. It's basic, simple, commitment-free and achieves its laudable if unexciting goal of ticking all of the boxes.
But this device costs the same as a Garmin Cirqa , a device I didn't think was all that amazing, but did a lot of these basics better. The Cirqa is at least equipped with the fundamentals you'd expect from a company of Garmin's size and experience. Take automatic activity tracking, for example, which I'd say isn't just nice to have but an essential feature for even those of us who are sub-weekend warriors.
If the SL-1 was cheaper, I'd have more positive things to say about it, because you could easily see it as a My First Whoop . But for this sort of money, I'd say there are better alternatives, even when you factor in additional subscription fees.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
articles.title_zh: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of people were reported to be in isolation after a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and other infectious diseases died of an undisclosed illness.
The researcher, a 28-year-old female laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration was watching the situation closely .
“I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it,” Rubio said.
Rospotrebnadzor has played down the link between the death of the researcher - named in local media as Darya Shipilova - and her work.
“No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it asserted, adding that the “epidemiological situation” in the region was stable.
Nevertheless, the agency’s head, Anna Popova, traveled to Irkutsk on Friday, according to the local governor, Igor Kobzev, for what he described as an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission.
The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region”, Kobzev said on Telegram.
Reached by phone on Monday, the institute where the researcher worked told CNN it was not commenting on the incident .
Regional authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” according to Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in eastern Russia, near the Mongolian border.
The inpatient facility at the hospital where the worker was treated has been placed under quarantine, and several departments have stopped discharging or admitting patients, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also been closed, according to local media reports.
The woman’s death was confirmed by officials last week.
Ekaterina, a resident of Shekelov, told CNN on Monday that there were no visible changes in the city, but locals were anxious. “My acquaintances are slightly panicking,” she said.
Another resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said he was “shocked” by the news.
Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, have said that nearly 200 people are under observation.
There have been no cases of infectious diseases reported among institute staff over the past 10 days, and all of the employee’s recent contacts are being tested and examined, Modin said.
In its only comment on the incident, the Kremlin said people should only trust updates coming from the official agency.
“One should rely on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than listening to various rumors and speculation,”  Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday.
The World Health Organization told CNN it was in contact with the Russian health authorities to “verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results.”
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” it said.
Despite such reassurances, Kyrgyzstan, which is some 1,500 miles from Irkutsk, announced Monday it was introducing quarantine controls at state border crossing points.
A virologist in Siberia, Alexander Chepurnov, told CNN that the strict protocols being followed were designed to prevent onward spread.
“After any suspected exposure, staff are instructed to immediately report it, decontaminate, undergo medical assessment and be isolated in a separate dedicated facility” for however long they might be infectious,” Chepirnov said.
If she had been working with something like the plague and hadn’t completed the required quarantine, “she would have been obliged to contact her own medical team…and under no circumstances should she have gone to a regular hospital,” he added.
Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization, told CNN that while pneumonic plague is deadly, it is not very transmissible and one would have to be exposed to a high viral load to become sick.
In that sense, it is unlike respiratory illnesses such as COVID, she said.
There is endemic plague among wildlife in parts of Siberia, Rassmussen added.
According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East.
The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee died “possibly from the plague,” but noted there had been no outbreak of the disease in his region.
Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues.
An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, noted “conflicting reports” were circulating and called for calm.
Oldest known evidence of plague reveals the disease’s deadly impact 5,500 years ago
The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday.
Onishchenko told state news agency TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission.
A US State Department spokesperson told CNN Sunday that it was aware of the possible death due to pneumonic plague in Russia.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” the spokesperson said. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The World Health Organization notes that the plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics if caught early.

articles.title_orig: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.title_zh: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.content_orig:
PRESS RELEASE — The second international Quantum Datacenter Alliance (QDA) Forum highlighted the progress towards commercial deployments and acceleration of distributed quantum computing architectures, while also outlining the next critical areas of focus for progress.
At the iconic Battersea Power Station, London, the QDA brought together technical, business, and government leaders to address one of the most pressing technical and ecosystem challenges: how to integrate emerging quantum hardware into existing and future data center infrastructure.
The agenda explored how quantum systems are moving from lab-scale demonstrations toward commercial deployment, highlighting that system level architecture, control, error correction, interoperability and power consumption have become as critical as the qubits themselves. Attendees also emphasised the importance of open sharing, interoperability, and collective thinking about the direction and future uses of quantum technologies.
Dr. Carmen Palacios-Berraquero, Founder and CEO of Nu Quantum said, “As quantum computing moves towards large-scale utility, collaboration becomes critical. The QDA brings the industry together to tackle the shared challenges of building quantum computing as infrastructure — scalable, interoperable, reliable and efficient — and ultimately making quantum compute accessible to the world, responsibly.”
Dame Wendy Hall, speaking about lessons from classical computing and AI,said, “It’s all about communication. It is so important to get the positive messages out about any new technology ahead of the inevitable scare stories about the risks and potential harms which the media love to pick up on. Of all the new technologies on the horizon though. Quantum computing is the hardest to explain to non technical audiences. That messaging will need a lot of work as the technology begins to emerge into the public arena.”
Hannah Boardman, Director responsible for AI, Quantum, Engineering Biology, Semiconductors, Robotics, Department for Science, Innovation & Technology , said, “Initiatives like this QDA show the power of bringing together different sections of the ecosystem across technologies, thinking in a different kind of way and focusing on delivering common goals to be identified in the room.”
Petrina Anne Steele, Head of Emerging Technologies at Equinix , said, “Quantum is an incubating technology that sits alongside classical HPC and now AI environments, and is highly complementary. Hybrid infrastructure is making quantum commercially actionable today. We already have companies doing high precision molecular modelling and exploring FX trading optimisation.”
Ben Bloom, Founder and CEO at Atom Computing , said, “Over the past two days, Nu Quantum and its partners have been exploring how to integrate quantum systems into a data center. This is an incredibly important topic as we continue to expand the reach of quantum computers to more and more industries and more and more users. Building a utility scale quantum computer doesn’t just fall to one company, and doesn’t even just fall to one technology. It’s the combination of multiple components together that will actually bring out a utility scale quantum computer.”
Looking ahead, the QDA will continue to convene industry leaders through future forums, working groups, and events, driving the industry toward scalable, robust, commercially viable quantum computing.

Beyond foundational computing, IBM possesses a deep legacy in aerospace and defense from building the guidance computers and Instrument Unit for NASA's historic Apollo missions to partnering with Airbus on CIMON, the first AI assistant on the ISS.

Their extensive product range serves various industrial, commercial, and scientific applications, making their technology integral to numerous sectors and industries.
Equinix specializes in digital infrastructure, operating a global network of data centers that provide colocation, connectivity, and managed solutions for enterprises, cloud providers, and network service providers. The company enables direct, secure interconnection between partners and platforms, supporting mission-critical applications, AI workloads, and hybrid multicloud environments. Equinix emphasizes reliability, scalability, and compliance, serving over 10,000 customers worldwide and facilitating digital transformation through its extensive ecosystem and advanced infrastructure.

The new department is responsible for helping to encourage, develop and manage the UK's scientific, research, and technological outputs. DSIT is also responsible for managing the necessary physical and digital infrastructure and regulation to support the British economy, UK public services, national security, and wider UK Government priorities.

The DSIT has launched a National Quantum Strategy, which is a 10-year vision and actions for the UK to be a leading quantum-enabled economy, recognizing the importance of quantum technologies for the UK's prosperity and security.
