articles.title_orig: UN upholds housing as a human right on World Habitat Day
articles.title_zh: UN upholds housing as a human right on World Habitat Day
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Representatives from governments, civil society and academia meeting in Muscat, Oman on Monday called for urgent action to address a global housing crisis affecting nearly 3.4 billion people.
They gathered to commemorate World Habitat Day which this year focuses on the theme of Adequate Housing for All.
“Adequate housing is not a luxury. It is a foundation for a dignified life and for sustainable cities,” said Anacláudia Rossbach, Executive Director of UN-Habitat , the agency that promotes sustainable urbanization.
She stressed that “housing needs to be treated as a public priority alongside land and basic services”, underlining the need for greater investment in communities and cooperation across government, the private sector and civil society.
In his message for the day, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called adequate housing for all “the foundation of dignity, security, and opportunity.”
He noted, however, that more than three billion people worldwide are denied this universal human right.
“Over one billion live in informal settlements and slums, and many more experience homelessness or have been displaced by conflict, disasters, and climate change,” he added.
The President of the United Nations Habitat Assembly, Nga Kor Ming, reminded participants that behind the numbers are real people.
Mr. Ming – Malaysia’s Minister of Housing and Local Government – highlighted the plight of families living in homes without legal protection, or even basic sanitation and clean water, whose children suffer preventable diseases.
“A house without clean water, safety or legal security is not a home. It is a poverty trap,” he said in a video message.  “Therefore, to deliver adequate housing for all, we must move away from quick fixes to systemic transformation.”
Ms. Rossbach explained that under the UN human rights framework , housing is considered adequate when it meets seven criteria that include availability of services, habitability, affordability, location and accessibility.
“Adequate housing means much more than a physical structure with four walls and a roof,” she said.
“A family may have a roof and still spend so much on rent that there is little left for food, education, or healthcare. A home may be affordable, but located far from jobs, schools, or transport.”
The UN Secretary-General upheld that “investing in adequate housing and transforming informal settlements reduces poverty, tackles inequality, builds climate resilience, and fosters peaceful and inclusive societies.”
He called for coordinated action by national and local governments, building stronger partnerships, and better use of data in decision-making.
“The international financial architecture must also be reformed to mobilize the adequate, predictable, and affordable financing developing countries need to invest in housing at scale,” he added.
The Secretary-General ended his message with an appeal to the international community.
“On this World Habitat Day, let us treat housing as a public good and build a world where everyone has a place to call home,” he said.
World Habitat Day is observed annually on the first Monday in October.
It marks the start of UN-Habitat’s Urban October – a month-long campaign to advocate for housing and sustainable urban development that concludes on World Cities Day , 31 October.

articles.title_orig: Season of Creation closes—but actions will continue
articles.title_zh: Season of Creation closes—but actions will continue
articles.content_orig:
As the Season of Creation officially closed on 4 October, people gathered online from across the world for a prayer service that not only recapped many green initiatives but also encouraged ongoing action to care for creation.
Speakers reflected on this year ’ s theme, "Living Water" (Ezekiel 47:9, 12): "Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live . . . Their fruit will be for food and their leaves for healing" (NRSV).
Analisa Ramsahai, environmental scientist and Catholic climate activist from Trinidad and Tobago, who serves as a board director and secretary for the global Laudato Si' Movement, focused on water as connection—our connection with each other, with the earth, and with God. “ Rain returns water to the earth, nourishing plants, animals and people,” she said. “ But before we explore these connections, I invite you to experience water for a moment.”
She then invited those gathered to imagine—and deeply appreciate—all the ways in which water touches their lives.
Elizabeth Trice, a UK-based wildlife and conservation professional and an active environmental organizer within the Church of England, and founder of “ The Seedlings Network,” expressed her appreciation for the gathering. “ It ’ s key to look back at our beginnings,” she said, referring to water being connected with the origins of all life.
“ It ’ s also important to remember that the voices of tomorrow are also the voices of today,” she added, noting that young people are not just carrying the future of the earth but also the present.
Fr Movses (Garen) Yosolkanian, Armenian Apostolic, with the Middle East Council of Churches (MECC), noted that water is a gift from God, a source of life, healing, and restoration. “ Yet we find ourselves in a thirsty moment in the struggle for global ecological justice,” he said. “ Across the world, our water sources are threatened. What should be a source of life is increasingly becoming a source of struggle, injustice, and division.”
Marí a Jos é Tejedor Gonz ález, with the ACT Alliance, thanked the speakers, those who began and continued earth-friendly initiatives, and all those who prayed. “ You all inspire us with your wisdom, hope, and witness throughout this season,” she said. “ You remind us that caring for creation is a shared calling. Although today marks the end of this year ’ s celebration, the journey continues.”
Season of Creation is the ecumenical world's month of prayer and action for creation. Beginning with “Feast of Creation in Christ” on 1 September, is a time of witness to God ’ s love and our human responsibility.
The season forms one chapter in the World Council of Church's Ecumenical Decade of Climate Justice Action (2025–2034), launched in Johannesburg in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Why airfares could rise even more, but airline profits won't
articles.title_zh: Why airfares could rise even more, but airline profits won't
articles.content_orig:
Volatile fuel prices and resilient travel demand are threatening to keep airfare high this year. Airline profits will be harder to come by.
The Iran war that began at the end of February sent fuel prices to multi-year if not record highs, including for diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, airlines' biggest expense after labor. Supply scares with the Strait of Hormuz disruptions lasting most of this year and high demand have sent jet fuel prices and other distilled products up more than crude oil.
Airline executives aren't expecting much relief in fuel costs anytime soon, or a drop in travel demand.
"You can't run the business on the hope that the Strait of Hormuz is going to open at a certain time," Qantas Airways CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in an interview late last month. The Australian airline operates some of the world's longest flights and is planning even longer ones for next year and 2028, starting routes between London and Sydney and New York and Sydney.
"There's a backdrop of resilient demand in in this environment. We're making sure that we've got our capacity settings right," she said.
Airlines have been passing higher fuel costs along to consumers by raising fares, adding fuel surcharges or increasing their checked baggage fees . The United States' on-again-off-again truce talks with Iran since the spring have kept fuel prices volatile, but airlines are holding onto those fare gains as customers continue to book.
Carriers have also raced to add more luxurious seats on board to capitalize on demand for pricier and roomier offerings, sometimes taking down the number of standard coach seats to do so.
Slightly fewer people are flying this year compared with last, but demand overall remains strong, even with higher ticket prices. Security screenings at U.S. airports were down 1% this year through Sept. 20 compared with the same period of 2025, according to a Sept. 23 Bernstein note.
Still, the latest U.S. inflation read showed airfare rose 23.4% in August from a year earlier. Holiday travel could be up even more. As of Sept. 24, fare-tracking platform Hopper said domestic, round-trip tickets were going for $402 over Thanksgiving, up 31% from last year. U.S. Christmas fares, meanwhile, are up 23% at $452 a round-trip.
Those holiday visits are essential to many families, said Hopper economist Hayley Berg, so a lot of flyers might not like the fare but book it anyway. Berg said many customers have been locking in their Thanksgiving and Christmas flights earlier than usual.
While business travel demand has been strong in recent months and off-peak trips are no longer a savvy traveler's secret, customers' focus on those key holiday trips this year could mean there are deals in the interim, Berg said.
"To me, that signals that they're already thinking about end of year travel and not thinking about any of those filler trips, fall shoulder-season trips," she said.
Carriers are forecasting double-digit revenue growth for the third quarter as customers spend more. That's even with slightly fewer people flying.
"I've never seen in my career, outside of recovery after maybe the pandemic or 9/11 ... seen a revenue environment in terms of year-over-year improvement," American Airlines CEO Robert Isom said at a Morgan Stanley investor conference last month. The carrier has been revamping its cabins to add more premium seats and other changes to catch up to rivals.
But despite the higher fares, Wall Street analysts have cut their profit estimates for U.S. carriers since another hike in jet fuel in the summer.
American in July said it expects to lose between 10 and 70 cents a share, on an adjusted basis, for the third quarter and cut its profit outlook for 2026.
Investors and anyone looking to buy a plane ticket in the next few months will get an updated view of what's to come when airline earnings season kicks off on Friday with Delta Air Lines . The most profitable U.S. carrier, which also stands to benefit from its owned refinery, will report third-quarter results and will give a fresh outlook for the end of the year.
Wall Street's focus will be on the fourth quarter and beyond. Airlines are likely to lower their earnings outlooks for that quarter, said Savanthi Syth, airline analyst at Raymond James.
She said carriers aren't likely to make as many broad-based fare increases now, but if jet fuel remains in the $4 to $4.50 a gallon range, they're likely to cut more flights, which can end up raising fares with customers facing fewer seats to choose from.
"You're going to see more rationalization in capacity," she said.
Volatile fuel costs are keeping airlines cautious. Carriers have trimmed some of their schedules to cut unprofitable or underperforming routes.
Along with fewer routes, the collapse of budget carrier Spirit Airlines in May took 1% to 2% of capacity out of the U.S. market, according to Barclays, meaning low-cost and full-service airlines alike have enjoyed more pricing power this year.
But should oil prices fall, investors will be watchful of whether airlines increase capacity in a big way, which could end up driving fares lower.
"We expect higher booked fares should result in similar unit revenue trends in the fourth quarter for most airlines, but elevated domestic capacity growth at American and United (+10% and +9% in current schedules) will likely be the most watched guidance by investors," Barclays airline analyst Brandon Oglenski said in a note Sept. 28. "With elevated energy prices and refining margins for jet fuel persisting, we expect capacity growth ambitions will be meaningfully curtailed by most management teams, with some potentially providing early expectations on 2027 planning assumptions."

articles.title_orig: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.title_zh: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.content_orig:
After a volcano erupted on tiny Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, the 264 displaced islanders told the BBC about their first taste of modern British life.
"Just over a year ago, they'd never seen traffic or a road or a house higher than a cottage," said Tim Brinton in a 1963 BBC programme. He was talking about the residents of Tristan da Cunha, the world's most remote inhabited island. In the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly halfway between Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, the tiny British outpost is more than 1,500 miles from any other populated land, and is only accessible by a seven-day boat journey.
But on 10 October 1961, a sudden volcanic eruption blasted the islanders out of their splendid isolation and into the industrialised modern world. "We heard the rumbles first, then the ground just automatically cracked… Then the smoke and the fire started coming out the ground," one of them told the BBC in a 1998 film. Another, Mary Swain, said that she'd run to her husband and shouted, "Jump up quick, Fred, the Earth is opening!"
The island's volcano had been dormant since Tristan was first settled 150 years earlier. But great cracks appeared in the ground a few hundred metres from the main village, which is named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. By the time the islanders had escaped in their fishing boats to nearby Nightingale Island, their homes were already threatened by lava. "The whole place is vibrating with earthquakes," announced a BBC reporter, "and the eastern corner is cracking and breaking up."
Tristan's 264 inhabitants were forced to evacuate , picked up by a Dutch liner that happened to arrive the next day. Within hours, the whole community was aboard, leaving everything apart from the few things they could carry with them – "a rifle, an overcoat and a lamp," recalled Swain – and their boats, which they stored in their gardens when they reached England weeks later.
They were housed on a disused military airbase near Southampton, a port city on England's south coast. "So much is strange to them," said Brinton. "They'd never seen shops because on the island, money wasn't used. Boats were their livelihood. For them, there's been no industrial revolution. And for 150 years, they've lived simple agricultural lives out of touch with world progress."
Though Tristan da Cunha was discovered in 1506 by a Portuguese admiral who gave it his name, it was another 300 years before it supported anything but seabirds and seals. The UK annexed the island in 1816 to prevent it being used as a base for attempts to free Napoleon Bonaparte from his imprisonment on the South Atlantic island of St Helena . The following year, a Scotsman, Corporal William Glass, stayed behind when the British garrison was withdrawn. With his family and a few others, he founded the first permanent community.
In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter.
By 1961, the population of the 40 sq miles (100 sq km) of volcanic rock had risen to 264, many of them survivors from ships wrecked on the island, with just seven family names between them. On several occasions, the failure of the potato crop or the wrecking of fishing boats brought the islanders to the point of starvation. But they stayed on, even defying several attempts by the British government to evacuate them.
When the volcanic eruption forced the islanders to leave, they faced difficulties settling in England. They had never seen a car, a bicycle, a TV set or an income tax form. And it was a challenging climate. "Here is too much gas and smoke," Tristanian Joey Repetto told the BBC in 1963. On his journey to their initial accommodation, he said, "I steady coughed without stopping."
Adapting to the nine-to-five work pattern also proved tricky for the community of farmers and fishermen. "Here, when you go to work in the morning, you've got one job. You've got to look forward all the whole week of getting up at the same time, going to the same place, doing the same work every day," said Joey's father Gerald, who was used to a more varied life determined by natural rhythms.
Similarly, financial pressures placed new demands on the islanders, as Swain explained. "In England, you need money for your living. But on Tristan, we don't. If we haven't got no money, well, we just go without it. It don't bother us at all… if I've got no money, I still can go out and get my own potatoes. I can still go and get my own fish."
She didn't hold back on expressing her views on British life. "We don't like the weather... There's too much sickness and we don't like the place at all."

Despite having a single policeman on the island, who wore a British uniform, Tristan had almost no crime. The community was shocked by an incident in England when one member was attacked and hurt by two youths, who took his most valued possession, a gold watch, and smashed it.
But there were some elements of British life that were appreciated by the Tristanians, particularly the younger ones, who described a love of Italian suits and record players. "Country and western music is our favourite, by Johnny Cash and Ernest Tubb," said one teenager, who also enjoyed the social dances. "Since I come here, I've been doing the twist and the locomotion, all that lot. We've forgotten how to do the waltz. But I like to twist myself."
Despite that, most of the islanders were keen to return home. In 1962, the British government sent a survey party to study conditions on Tristan. While the volcano was still smoking, the geologists judged that it was now dormant.
Surprisingly little damage had been done to the village of Edinburgh. The lava had turned at the last moment and flowed into the sea, something that the islanders considered to be an act of God. Some of the thatched roofs were burnt, but the cottages were mostly intact. Yet in their absence, houses had been ransacked and some livestock stolen by passing sailors.
Many animals were still alive, however, with the chickens multiplying in number. Though the dogs had run wild and slaughtered the sheep, the cattle had kept themselves well-fed on the lush island grass, and there were new calves. Lava had covered the beaches, but return was possible.
The British authorities held a secret ballot in the community hall at the islanders' RAF camp. All Tristanians over the age of 21 voted, and the result was an almost unanimous vote to return, 148 to five in favour. After an advance party went back to plant seeds for the following year's potato crop, most of the islanders arrived at Tristan da Cunha in November 1963.
When asked what she was most looking forward to on the island when she returned, Swain told the BBC: "A free life. We can get our own fish and everything of our own back there without money."
Elaine Repetto, who was born on the island but chose to leave in 1984, told the BBC in 1998 why it held such a pull. "We are strongly independent and used to battling with the elements in order to survive… We have to rely upon each other in a way you would find in few other places."
She described the impact of the events in 1961. "Today, the volcano is still a smoking reminder of the events which shaped our view of ourselves and our contact with the outside world."

articles.title_orig: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.title_zh: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.content_orig:
UCSF’s $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital is scheduled to open in 2030, but it wont’t fix the university’s staffing crisis, write Drs. Akshar Rambachan and Anand Habib.
Every day, we watch our patients and fellow physicians pay the price for a strained system we didn’t build and can’t fix alone.
We are doctors at UCSF. At UCSF’s flagship Parnassus Hospital, people sick enough to need a hospital room wait on gurneys in emergency-room hallways because there aren’t enough staffed hospital beds.
We see patients attached to IV antibiotics laying on beds outside ER bathrooms. Elderly patients with hip fractures and pain languish under bright lights and constant noise until, deprived of sleep, they develop delirium. Families are forced to discuss end-of-life wishes within earshot of strangers in the hallway.
These are the daily realities at what should be a world-class health-care system. It’s a patient-care crisis driven by a dysfunctional system that we, as doctors, had no hand in building — or get a say in changing.
For generations, doctors had the authority and independence to make structural staffing choices to deliver high-quality patient care. Physicians owned practices, allowing them to control their patient load and shape the staffing team.
That world is disappearing. Physicians increasingly work as employees of sprawling health systems in which decisions about staffing, workload, compensation and budgets are made further and further from the bedside.
Whatever the administrators are doing clearly isn’t working. UCSF’s emergency wait time is more than 20% higher than the national average .
When UCSF patients are finally seen, their average length of patient stay is 60% higher than the state average — which strongly correlates with negative patient outcomes .
The Parnassus ER has more than double the national average of patients who leave without seeing doctors.
As doctors, we write emails, join committees, conduct studies and share proposals shaped by our years of training, research and experience to address this crisis. Our reports, requests, complaints and proposals are treated as suggestions and all but ignored.
That is why we and physicians across the University of California system are organizing a union.
She’s a longtime Democratic officeholder, but she sounds like a Main Street conservative in her campaign for the state’s No. 2 job
Following concerns over how sensitive information is accessed, mayor’s new rules would shorten data retention, require documented searches and add oversight
Annual celebration of the US Navy is zooming back into The City for seven days of festivities and the return of the elite flight squad
UCSF’s solution to the patient care crisis is the $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital, scheduled to open in 2030. Let us be clear — we support the new hospital. Parnassus needs more critical inpatient and emergency rooms, and our patients deserve modern facilities.
But fancy new buildings don’t treat patients — people do. The expansion can’t be a substitute for solving the real crisis: the decreased investment in frontline staffing, resulting in chronic shortages that make it impossible to provide patients with world-class care.
We are often told that capital spending and staffing come from different budgetary “pots.” The accounting may separate capital and operating expenses, but the underlying finances are interconnected. UC’s own debt policy makes that clear: Medical centers seeking external financing must demonstrate adequate operating income, cash on hand and the ability to cover their debt payments .
In other words, financing what UCSF builds for tomorrow depends on the operating performance of the health system today — which is to say, on the people doing the work.
You cannot grow a system by hollowing out the front-line workers who make it run. Commitments to adequate staffing, sustainable workloads, and retention of the people required to operate new hospitals should not be revisited every budget cycle, revocable with every change in leadership. They should be codified and fixed to maintain continuity and quality.
To deliver on our mission to do everything in our power to get the best outcomes for our patients, doctors need a say not only in how we provide care, but also in the conditions within which that care happens.
We need mechanisms to ensure sufficient staffing at all levels, guardrails on how technology is used in patient care, and safe worksites that support healthy outcomes for our patients — not wait times that cause suffering and worsen their symptoms.
Through the UC Physicians Committee, doctors across specialties and campuses are organizing with University Professional and Technical Employees union, alongside many of the pharmacists, therapists and other professionals we already work with every day.
Together, we can codify common-sense policies so that every part of a patient’s care team is set up for success.
The Helen Diller Hospital is a promise about what UCSF intends to be in 2030. The medical professionals caring for San Franciscans today deserve a binding voice in what it is now. A union is how we get one, so that the institution we’re proud to work for can be the one that its patients were promised.
Dr. Akshar Rambachan is a hospital-medicine physician at UCSF. Dr. Anand Habib is an internal-medicine physician at UCSF.

FILE - Britain's Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, looks round as he leaves after attending the Easter Matins Service at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, England, April 20, 2025. Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP hide caption
LONDON — The former Prince Andrew has filed a legal action challenging the warrants that authorized searches at two of his homes earlier this year as British police investigated allegations related to his links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A judicial spokesperson confirmed that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had filed a claim with the High Court in London and a hearing is scheduled for Thursday.
The Daily Telegraph previously reported that Mountbatten-Windsor had asked the court to determine whether Thames Valley Police acted lawfully in searching the former prince's homes near Windsor Castle and on King Charles III's Sandringham estate.
The searches were conducted in February when Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that the former prince shared sensitive information with Epstein during his time as the U.K.'s trade envoy.
Police questioned Mountbatten-Windsor for 11 hours before he was released under investigation, meaning he was neither charged nor exonerated.
It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal was placed under arrest, underscoring how deference to the monarchy has eroded in recent years.
Thames Valley Police said Monday that its investigation was continuing, even as it confirmed that the department was involved in legal proceedings about the search warrants. A department spokesman declined further comment while those proceedings are underway.
The allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor came to light when the U.S. Justice Department released millions of pages of documents from its investigation into sex trafficking by Epstein and his connections to a network of wealthy, powerful men around the world.
Mountbatten-Windsor's relationship with Epstein has been a source of embarrassment to the royal family for more than a decade and forced him to give up royal duties in 2019.
But as further revelations began to leak out of the U.S. investigation last year, the king moved to insulate the monarchy from the fallout by stripping his younger brother of his princely title.
After Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested, Charles departed from the "never complain, never explain" approach of his late mother, Queen Elizabeth, and took the unusual step of issuing a statement on the investigation.
"Let me state clearly: the law must take its course,'' he said at the time. "As this process continues, it would not be right for me to comment further on this matter.''

articles.title_orig: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.title_zh: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.content_orig:
Climate change could make a number of infectious diseases worse. I expected malaria would be one of them.
That’s concerning, given the huge global burden that it already carries: it kills almost half a million children every year.
But a more complex story emerges from the scientific literature. One where rising temperatures could actually reduce the burden of malaria in some areas, while making it worse in others.
What impact has climate change already had on malaria? Will it make the global fight against it harder or easier in the future?
These are the questions that I want to answer here.
Before we look at how climate change could change the dynamics and distribution of malaria in the future, we need a quick primer on the global burden of the disease today.
This is important because climate change could cause a decline in malaria in some regions, while increasing the prevalence in others. The impact on the overall global burden of malaria will mostly depend on what happens in the worst-affected regions today.
Malaria is an infectious disease present across much of the tropics and subtropics. In the map below, you can see the band of new infections across South America, South and Southeast Asia, and Africa.
The difference between sub-Saharan Africa and other parts of the tropics, though, is huge. Infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa are around 100 times higher than in South America and 50 times higher than in South Asia.
The fact that severe malaria is mostly an African story today is even clearer when we look at where people die from it. More than 95% of the 600,000 people who die from malaria every year live in sub-Saharan Africa. You can see this regional breakdown below. 1
But this chart also makes clear that within sub-Saharan Africa, there are substantial differences in the burden.
Around half of global deaths occur in West Africa — countries like Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Liberia. The rest are split between the central and eastern parts of the continent. Southern Africa has extremely low rates of malaria.
This dominance in West Africa is not just about population (we might expect more deaths in denser areas). As you can see in this map of death rates , those living in West Africa are at a much higher risk of dying from malaria.
These are the important background facts to make sense of this article’s focus. Most deaths from malaria occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Within the continent, West Africa is hit the worst. And children are most at risk: tragically, around 70% of malaria deaths are among children. That’s almost half a million children dying of the disease every year.
To understand the link between malaria and climate change, we need to know the basics of the disease’s “perfect conditions”.
Several mosquito species in Africa carry and spread malaria. A dominant one is Anopheles gambiae . It carries and spreads the parasite Plasmodium falciparum , which is what infects humans.
Over many decades, scientists have studied the ideal conditions for these mosquitoes to thrive. The spread of malaria peaks in these species at around 25°C. 2 Transmission drops close to zero below 16°C and above 34°C.
That means the suitability of malaria forms a bell-shaped curve like the one below. It spreads best at 25°C; this suitability drops on either side of it, and eventually becomes negligible.
Temperature is not the only thing that matters. How established malaria already is in a given country or region does, too. As do rainfall patterns: female mosquitoes lay their eggs in standing water, and larvae need water to develop. So, rainfall creates favorable conditions for malaria to spread. There is a limit, though: heavy, persistent rain often washes larvae away, preventing them from developing. An area with moderate rainfall is therefore a good breeding ground for malaria to spread.
Humidity can also have an effect. Adult Anopheles dry out in low-humidity air, so they often live longer in wetter, more humid seasons (and when they live longer, they do a better job of spreading the parasite).
The world has already warmed by around 1.4°C since pre-industrial times. 3
What impact has this already had on the prevalence of malaria?
A recent paper by Colin Carlson and colleagues, published in Nature , estimated the impact of historical climate change on the burden of malaria so far, and projected how this might affect it in the future under different warming scenarios. 4 The paper focused on the burden on children in Africa — as we established earlier, this is the most affected demographic, both in terms of cases and deaths.
They estimate that over the last century — from 1901 to 2014 — climate change has led to a small increase in the prevalence of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa. By “increase”, they mean that rates were slightly higher than they would have been compared to a hypothetical scenario without climate change . The prevalence of malaria has actually declined in recent decades, but for reasons unrelated to climate.
Across the region, this increase was estimated at roughly 1 case per 1,000 children aged 2 to 10. To put this into context, around 24% of children (or 240 in every 1,000) in this region were estimated to carry the malaria parasite at the end of the study period. So, the overall impact has been relatively small and is quite uncertain. 59% of the study’s simulations showed an increase in malaria prevalence, with uncertainty ranging from a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 to an increase of 6 cases per 1,000.
The bigger impact has been in changing the prevalence of malaria across different parts of the continent. Hotter temperatures might not have led to a large increase, on average, but they have affected its distribution.
Climate change has probably led to a decline in malaria in West Africa, but an increase in the southern and eastern parts of the continent. The following map summarizes this change: you see blue in the West but red, marking an increase, in the East and South.
Remember that West Africa is where the burden of malaria has been, and still is, the highest. A decline there due to climate change has been almost entirely offset by an increase elsewhere on the continent, which is why the effect, on aggregate, is very small.
The chart below shows malaria prevalence in two scenarios: the realistic one the world has lived through, and an alternate reality without human-driven climate change. Malaria has declined in West Africa due to climate change, but has increased in the other three subregions.
To understand why climate change has made things better in West Africa, but worse elsewhere, let’s return to our bell-shaped curve of where malaria thrives.
The study by Carlson and colleagues found results very similar to previous studies on the optimal conditions for malaria-carrying mosquitoes: transmission peaks at around 25°C.
In 1901, the average temperature in West Africa was around 26°C — very close to, but just past, the ideal temperature. 5 Climate change has increased temperatures, pushing them away from the optimum and down the slope.
What has happened elsewhere? East and Central Africa started below the optimum, at around 22°C, and Southern Africa far below, at around 17°C. Higher temperatures in all of these regions have pushed them closer to the optimum. East and Central Africa now sit at around 24°C, and Southern Africa at around 18°C.
It’s this temperature effect that has driven these diverging patterns across sub-Saharan Africa. The authors of the study did not find a discernible signal of climate change in historical drought and flood trends.
What’s crucial is that, while climate change has, on net, probably increased the burden of malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, its impact has been small compared with the many interventions and investments made to control and alleviate malaria. Malaria cases and deaths have not increased, but fallen substantially over the longer term.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump vs. Bernie Sanders—2 Sharply Different Views of America’s Role in the World
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump vs. Bernie Sanders—2 Sharply Different Views of America’s Role in the World
articles.content_orig:
One is an imperial gangster; the other seeks to create a world “not based on greed but based on justice, on decency.”
America’s century is over. History has not ended. This has become the new conventional wisdom even among the keepers of convention.
The challenge is how America finds real security in this new era. This month, we witnessed two strikingly different answers: one from the self-proclaimed most powerful man in the world, Donald Trump, and one from the champion of the rising populist movement on the left, Senator Bernie Sanders.
Trump’s address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly was a characteristically grotesque performance, essentially a raised middle finger to the 190 country representatives gathered before him and the UN itself. Amid the routine farrago of lies, boasts, threats, and resentments, he presented a stark vision of America’s emerging role: essentially an imperial gangster—that, if pursued, constitutes a clear, present, and harrowing threat to this nation’s security.
After a stump speech preening about America’s primacy—“Our economy is the envy of the world. Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet”—Trump turned to America’s role in the world.
He boasted about the bombing of Iran, the “peace” in Gaza, the kidnapping of Venezuela’s president and control of its oil—“to the victor go the spoils”—the bombing of fishing boats in the Caribbean designated as “foreign terrorists,” the blockade of Cuba, “failing like never before and it will fail.”
Each of these—from aggressive acts of war to aiding and abetting genocide to illegal blockade—represent a brazen and open violation of international law and the UN Charter. Trump is saying that America will continue to police the world, only not to enforce the law but to enforce its will and to take what it can get. In apparent acknowledgment of the lawlessness, he issued a scurrilous attack on the International Criminal Court, “an evil group of people,” calling on all members to resign from the “rogue institution.”
Ironically, this fool’s errand of brazen plunder isn’t Trump’s greatest disservice to US national security. As the UN secretary general warned in his opening remarks, the world is struggling with the growing costs of real and present dangers that can no longer be ignored and can only be addressed by greater international cooperation: catastrophic climate change, global pandemics, corrosive inequality that undermines democracy and savages the poor, an accelerating nuclear arms race accompanied by the collapse of arms control agreements, and the known unknown of AI, which requires international regulation.
Trump made clear that the United States, under his watch, will sabotage any international regulation. Climate change and efforts to regulate AI are dismissed as a “hoax.” He has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization that monitors emerging pandemic threats and crippled our own Centers for Disease Control. Having pocketed billions while in office, he is the tribune of oligarchs, torpedoing all efforts at imposing a minimal tax on multinationals or on carbon or efforts to shut down tax-free zones. “There is no global government,” he preached, and “while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.” And, boasting about hiking America’s bloated military budget by one-third—to $1.5 trillion—and promising to build a “Global Dome” over America, he only adds fuel to the nuclear arms race.
At the dawn of the conservative era, Britain’s Margaret Thatcher asserted that “there was no alternative” to the neoliberal catechism. But there is an alternative course for the United States as it struggles to address new realities. It won’t come from a return to the failed “unipolar” globalism of the past decades. Instead, if there is an alternative to Trump’s gangsterism, it will come from the rising populist movement of the left.
Speaking on the eve of the UN General Assembly at Riverside Church in New York, Bernie Sanders offered a clear outline. He began with a tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King’s historic address at Riverside at the height of the Vietnam War, and his warning that “a nation that continues year after year to spend more money on military defense than on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death.”
He argued that not only is the US spending more and more on military weapons while turning its back on working people and the poor, but that “it is happening all over the world.”
To turn that around begins with a change in US policy, including “an end” to Trump’s “disastrous war on Iran,” termination of military aid to Israel and condemnation of “the genocide” in Gaza, work with grassroots activists to end “Putin’s disastrous war in Ukraine,” and denunciation of the UAE for aiding the genocide in Sudan’s civil war.
The growing violence, he argued, makes the United Nations more, not less, important, arguing that instead of arguing that “might makes right,” “our job is to strengthen the United Nations…and bring disagreements to the negotiating table…”
That would enable us to address the real and present security threats that we now face. At the top of that list, Sanders warns, is that “we are moving rapidly toward an extremely dangerous global oligarchy.” In nation after nation, we witness unprecedented levels of wealth and income inequality, illustrated by the fact that just as “the top 1 percent of America now owns more wealth than the bottom 94 percent,” the ratio is similar across the world.
“Children die of preventable diseases. People suffer every day. People give up hope. And 3,400 of the richest people on Earth became $4 trillion richer last year alone.”
Books & the Arts / Corey Robin
Leena Barakat and Pamela Shifman
The oligarchy, Sanders warned, “is ascending, working families are struggling to stay alive, and democracy is in retreat. The great challenge that we face in our country and all over the world is that that trend must be reversed.”
Sanders then turned to the other existential threats—focusing on the need to control the development of AI and to address catastrophic climate change.
The contrast is clear. For Trump, America strides the world. Our military will enforce our will. “The spoils” will go to the powerful, not to the people. Threats like AI and climate change are a “hoax.” International institutions are irrelevant if not evil.
For Sanders, militarism is a threat, not an answer. Basic security and democracy here and across the world are threatened primarily by an increasingly powerful and rapacious oligarchy. The emerging threats—climate change, AI (as well as pandemics and nuclear weapons, which he doesn’t mention)—require global cooperation. Changing our course depends not on building up the military but on building a progressive citizens movement here and across the world that can create a world “not based on greed but based on justice, on decency.”
Impossible? Perhaps, but Sanders reminds us of the “immortal words of Nelson Mandela: It always seems impossible until it is done.”

An expert on international affairs and US politics, she is an award-winning columnist and frequent contributor to The Guardian . Vanden Heuvel is the author of several books, including The Change I Believe In: Fighting for Progress in the Age of Obama , and co-author (with Stephen F. Cohen) of Voices of Glasnost: Interviews with Gorbachev’s Reformers .

articles.title_orig: The mispricing of war
articles.title_zh: The mispricing of war
articles.content_orig:
The true price of war is rarely paid by those who start it. In a deeply interconnected world economy, the financial burden of conflict is increasingly exported through inflation, disrupted trade and slowing growth worldwide
In the space of just a few weeks, the throttling of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has revealed the true nature of the US-Israeli war with Iran. This is no regional conflict, because the entire world is being invoiced. While the size of the bill remains to be determined, it is already obvious that the belligerents won’t be the only ones paying the tab. War is typically framed in terms of national security, territorial integrity, humanitarianism, or even civilisational struggle. But such rationales obscure an unsettling truth: war is one of the most mispriced of human activities. Those who initiate it rarely bear the full costs, which tend to be displaced across borders, markets and time. Beyond the physical destruction, war generates massive negative externalities. The price paid by the perpetrator reflects only a small fraction of the social cost.
Of course, the intuition that war imposes downstream costs on others is deeply embedded in the political-economy literature, running from Adam Smith and David Ricardo to John Maynard Keynes and Karl Polanyi. But globalisation has transformed the effect into a structural feature of the modern economy.
Economic growth diminishing Consider the arithmetic of the current Iran conflict. Beyond the loss of life, direct US military spending may run into the tens or even hundreds of billions of dollars. Yet the broader economic cost – transmitted through energy, food and financial markets – runs far higher. The International Monetary Fund warns that the war is already diminishing many economies’ growth prospects, as energy shocks ripple outward and inflationary pressures intensify.
The transmission mechanism is brutally simple. When oil and gas prices rise, transportation and electricity become more expensive. When fertiliser costs increase, so do food prices. Central banks may respond by assuming a tighter monetary-policy stance. Ultimately, growth slows. Yet this domino effect is missing from the actual war ledger. Efforts to measure the true costs of war have consistently found that they lie beyond the battlefield. In their work on the Iraq war, Joseph Stiglitz and Linda Bilmes tallied a catalogue of costs in the trillions of dollars once macroeconomic effects were included. Similarly, both the IMF and the World Bank have found that violent conflict depresses growth in economies far removed from it.
Even under conservative assumptions, the US may bear only a modest share of the total global economic damage (much as the negative spillovers of the war in Ukraine far exceed the direct cost to Russia). As European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde recently cautioned, the rest is diffused across the system, absorbed by energy importers, emerging markets and households worldwide. War, in this sense, is globally subsidised.
Three mechanisms make this possible. The first is spatial. Modern economies are deeply interconnected. When war disrupts one node (particularly an energy chokepoint), the effects cascade outward. The Strait of Hormuz is not simply a geographic passage but a structural vulnerability in the global economy. The second mechanism is temporal. War typically requires the present to borrow from the future. Governments finance conflict through debt, deferring its cost to generations not yet politically represented. The fiscal consequences of past wars continue to unfold decades later, showing up in public debt, constrained policy options, and obligations that outlast the politics that created them.
The third mechanism is distributive. War concentrates decision-making while dispersing the costs. Those who decide are not the ones who pay. This last insight lies at the heart of modern conflict economics. The Oxford University economist Paul Collier has shown that wars persist not because they are collectively rational, but because they are privately beneficial. Small groups capture the gains as the broader population absorbs the losses. Today’s networked economy amplifies this asymmetry.
When the world pays the price As Edward Fishman of the Centre on Global Energy Policy argues in his book Chokepoints, power today flows through global systems such as energy routes, financial networks and supply chains. But conflict turns these into channels for economic contagion. The result is a peculiar inversion. War appears expensive in theory but affordable in practice, because much of the bill is paid by others. This mispricing has predictable consequences. When goods are subsidised, we get more of them. When their price is too low, we get oversupply: too much pollution, too much risk and too much war.
The policy challenge is therefore familiar, even if the politics are not: to discourage war, its costs must be internalised. Those who initiate conflict must bear a greater share (or, even better, the entirety) of its true costs. Ensuring that outcome requires an effective global institution that can align the private and social costs of conflict more effectively than global markets can. Until the world can come up with such an institution, the incentives will remain perverse, because one of the most destructive activities imaginable seems so affordable to those who undertake it.

articles.title_orig: How the Midterms Could Complicate the Supreme Court’s New Term
articles.title_zh: How the Midterms Could Complicate the Supreme Court’s New Term
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court’s new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.
Here’s a look at what’s in store:
The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case . The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.
Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.
The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren’t the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.
About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.
Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.
The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.
The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump’s wide-reaching crackdown.
One is about deportations of migrants who can’t be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.
The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.
The other case is over the administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they’ve been in the country for years.
The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.
A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.
One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.
It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.
Catholic preschools that can’t take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It’s the justices’ latest case involving religious rights.
St. Mary Catholic Parish says it’s been left out of the state’s universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.
Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

articles.title_orig: Then and Now: World War I cenotaph
articles.title_zh: Then and Now: World War I cenotaph
articles.content_orig:
The 13th celebration of Armistice Day in Spokane is remembered for some monumental events.
Although it was a Tuesday, almost all businesses in downtown Spokane closed in honor of the day’s schedule. Most notable was the 12:30 p.m. unveiling of the 12-foot bronze statue of President Abraham Lincoln on a pedestal at Main Avenue and Monroe Street, surrounded by thousands who had just watched the Armistice Day parade. Among the attendees was one of the last Civil War veterans of the region.
But earlier that same day, Spokane’s American Legion Post 9 dedicated a solemn stone cenotaph at Riverside Cemetery, now called Riverside Memorial Park. The 19-by-26-foot platform, made from granite quarried in the Dishman area, consisted of a speaker’s rostrum surrounded by a wall lined with benches and an 8-foot arched stone with the inscription: “In Memory of Those Who Gave Their Lives for their Country in the World War.”
Legion member and architect Henry Bertelsen designed the monument and stonecutter Julian Mosfelt Simonson, also a member, carved the stone. As is typical with a cenotaph, meaning “empty tomb,” no names are inscribed there.
During the war from 1914-18, 11,000 Spokane men served in the military, more than 4,000 went to Europe and almost 200 men from Spokane died in the war.
Almost 500 people attended the dedication, where tearful Gold Star mothers took seats on the cold stone benches surrounding the platform while veterans and families gathered around.
The American Legion was founded in 1919 by the weary veterans of the war in Europe. From its inception, the Legion endeavored to honor past military service, including those from the Civil War and the Spanish -American War. The group would also advocate for veterans benefits and  comfort the bereaved.
Both built in 1920, the Argonne Road bridge and Marne Bridge over Latah Creek were dedicated to returning war veterans, but Legion members wanted to do more. The veterans sold poppies and held other fundraisers to raise the $7,500 to build the memorial, which would be situated near veterans’ burial areas so the platform could be used for future burials.
Some 20 years after the 1930 dedication, an “S” was added to the inscription, changing “World War” to “Wars.”

articles.title_orig: Former Avalanche Forward Is Lighting The World On Fire Since Returning To Vegas
articles.title_zh: Former Avalanche Forward Is Lighting The World On Fire Since Returning To Vegas
articles.content_orig:
Victor Olofsson left Vegas looking for a fresh start.
A little more than a year later, he's back with the Golden Knights and off to a pretty good start.
Olofsson scored on the power play in Sunday's 3-2 win over the Vancouver Canucks. That gave him two goals and an assist through three games, putting him at a point per game to open the season. He's also fired seven shots on net.
It's not a huge sample, but it's certainly an encouraging one for a player who has bounced around a bit since leaving Vegas after the 2024-25 season.
Olofsson spent most of last season with the Colorado Avalanche. He played 60 games, scored 11 goals and finished with 25 points. One of those goals was the first hat trick of his NHL career, which came against the Blackhawks on Oct. 28.
His time in Colorado ended when he was sent to Calgary as part of the trade that brought Nazem Kadri back to the Avalanche. Olofsson didn't spend long with the Flames, playing 18 games and picking up six points before free agency came around.
Vegas was interested again.
The Golden Knights signed Olofsson to a one-year deal on July 1, giving him another shot with the team he had left the previous summer.
There was some history there. Olofsson scored three goals in his first four games during his first stint with Vegas, only to suffer a lower-body injury that kept him out for nearly two months.
Now he's back, healthy and getting opportunities on the power play.
His third-line role at even strength isn't anything particularly notable, but that's not necessarily where Olofsson needs to make his living. He's always been more interesting as an offensive player, and Vegas has given him chances to use that skill with the man advantage.
For the Avalanche, Olofsson's start is worth keeping an eye on. He wasn't a major piece in Colorado, but he was productive enough to finish with 25 points in 60 games and gave the team some offense in a depth role.
Now he's three games into his return to Vegas and already has three points.
Maybe a fresh start was exactly what Olofsson needed.

articles.title_zh: Monday is World Teachers’ Day, honoring educators and marking 60-year milestone
articles.content_orig:
BEND, Ore. (KTVZ) -- Students and families across Central Oregon can join people around the world Monday in recognizing the educators who help children learn, grow, and prepare for their futures.
World Teachers’ Day is observed each year on October 5th to celebrate teachers and draw attention to the support, training, and working conditions they need to succeed.
The date commemorates the adoption of the 1966 International Labour Organization and UNESCO Recommendation Concerning the Status of Teachers. The landmark document established international standards related to teacher preparation, recruitment, employment, professional development, rights, and responsibilities.
This year’s observance marks the recommendation’s 60th anniversary. The 2026 theme is “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures.”
UNESCO says this year’s events will examine challenges affecting the status of teachers and call on communities and policymakers to protect, promote, and elevate the profession.
Teachers’ influence often extends well beyond lessons in reading, writing, math, and science. Educators also help students build confidence, explore career paths, solve problems, and navigate important stages of their lives.
For Central Oregon families, Monday offers a simple opportunity to thank a teacher, counselor, or other school employee who has made a difference.

articles.title_orig: Long Beach child hospitalized with rare disease related to West Nile virus
articles.title_zh: Long Beach child hospitalized with rare disease related to West Nile virus
articles.content_orig:
The boy first developed rashes before showing worse symptoms. Charisse Gibson reports for the NBC4 News at 4 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026.
A Southern California boy faces a potentially lengthy recovery after being hospitalized with West Nile virus, prompting his mother to warn other parents about the early signs as Los Angeles County sees a record number of mosquito-borne infections.
As 13-year-old Joseph Vasquez remains unable to walk while being treated at Los Angeles Children's Hospital, his mother, Maria Salazar, told NBC Los Angeles that she was fearful her son could die.
Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
It all started with a rash that looked like chickenpox, according to Salazar. Then Joseph took a fall at school before developing other symptoms, including a fever, loss of appetite and headaches.
"We ended up taking him to the emergency room because I found him facedown on the ground," the mother said, explaining that Joseph had been losing his balance before he was diagnosed with West Nile virus. "It just started to be from the lower body, and then he couldn't even feel his toes or movement."
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about 80% of West Nile virus infections are asymptomatic, while less than 1% of infected people develop neuroinvasive disease.
"Most of the cases, we have fever, maybe you just feel like funny," Dr. Ilan Shapiro of AltaMed Health Services said. "But there are cases, and that's why it's so important to talk about these viruses that can have problems, neurologically speaking, in our kids."
Shapiro, who is not Joseph's doctor, said inflammation caused by the infection may be making it challenging for the 13-year-old to walk.
"Our body is actually made of nerves and other things that actually connect our brain to our body. Sometimes that part of the connection can actually get inflamed, and that's where you can actually have this," the doctor explained.
Salazar, who initially thought her son had a common cold, now urges other parents to take proper precautions when kids go outdoors and pay attention to symptoms — the signs she initially brushed off.
"They should be looking out for any mosquito bites, dizziness, headaches, blurry vision, falling, losing balance," she said. "If your kids are telling you, 'Hey, my head hurts,' and they're scratching, take them to the doctor."
Dr. Shapiro said it's important to seek medical attention if people experience symptoms such as fever, chills, brain fog and fatigue, especially after spending time outdoors.
Los Angeles County has recorded 135 confirmed West Nile virus infections this year, including 130 hospitalizations and five deaths, according to the county Department of Public Health.

articles.title_orig: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.title_zh: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

articles.title_orig: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
articles.title_zh: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
articles.content_orig:
Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.
"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.
The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.
"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

articles.title_orig: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
articles.title_zh: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
articles.content_orig:
As trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood species
‘W hen I accidentally catch a shark, I bring it to my dogs,” Henrik Jensen, a 27-year-old from Greenland’s west coast, says casually. “I don’t let it back down because [the sharks] bully me and cut my lines.”
Jensen has fished for halibut in Ilulissat, Greenland’s third largest town, for a decade. He works an hour north of the town’s main iceberg-laden fishery, which sustains the livelihood of nearly 400 fishers. There, the halibut are bigger and more plentiful, but so are the Greenland sharks.
“This year I’ve lost around 6,000 hooks in total. Sometimes we lose 30,000 Danish krone [£3,440] a day,” says Jensen.
The Greenland shark is one of the least understood species on the planet. As well as being the world’s slowest shark, it is the second-largest carnivorous species, after the white shark, according to the Shark Trust . Reaching about six to seven metres in length, they can live for more than 400 years. For a long time they were thought to be completely blind, although scientists have recently discovered this may not be true .
The sharks inhabit a vast range across the deep and cold waters of the north and west Atlantic, but their attempts to feed on the northern fisheries’ main catch – Greenland halibut and Atlantic cod – often see them tangled in gear and brought in as bycatch.
This acrimonious coexistence has been documented ever since targeted fishing for the sharks’ liver oil ceased in the 1960s, but it came to a head earlier this year. The Avannaata municipality, of which Ilulissat is the administrative seat, approved a controversial plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering 300 krone for every heart of a Greenland shark.
Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of the municipality, says: “We need to safeguard the income of fishermen and the catch so that we can continue to eat the foods that we have relied on for generations.”
For many fishing inshore, working in small teams on dinghies, it brought a longstanding issue to a head. Timotheus Petersen, chair of the fishing association in Kullorsuaq, says: “Our longlines are expensive – one costs 1,599 krone. When the sharks cut our lines, we cannot finish fishing. We have to spend more money and buy new gear.”
The plan was eventually dropped after the government questioned its legality, but the prospect of a future cull remains.
In its decision to approve the cull, Avannaata council cited a similar scheme from the early 2000s in the former Aasiaat municipality, where a bounty of 200 krone was offered. According to a 2007 report from the Danish Technical University, another scheme between 1986 and 2001 in the former Uummannaq municipality brought in 19,697 hearts.
But the marine conservation group Oceans North Kalaallit Nunaat (ONKN) argues that culls do not resolve the issue, highlighting the migratory nature of the species, which can swim up to 1,200 miles (2,000km) a year. “Sharks removed in north-west Greenland would quickly be replaced by individuals arriving from other regions,” ONKN warned .
Many fishers also do not consider 300 krone worth the effort of hauling a shark onboard. “It’s difficult to catch them,” Jensen says. “You need bigger hooks and chains for the lines, so I don’t think anyone wants to try.”
But the debate around a possible cull is alarming conservationists. “If somebody says, ‘I’m going to cull a couple of thousand Greenland sharks’, that’s a disaster in my opinion,” says Prof Nick Dulvy, a marine conservationist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia.
The Greenland shark is believed to become sexually mature at 150, which means the species replaces itself extremely slowly and will not rebound from a cull quickly. It is still recovering from targeted fishing throughout the 19th and mid-20th centuries, when, at its peak in 1948, 58,000 were landed .
“They are probably – biologically – the most sensitive species in the ocean to overfishing,” Dulvy says. Globally, it is estimated that 3,500 sharks are caught every year as bycatch and the population remains in decline.
Greenland’s fishing community highlight their longstanding problem with the sharks, but do not say why it has suddenly escalated. Jenseeraq Poulsen, the director of ONKN, suggests it is due to mounting pressures within a fishing industry that accounts for about 25% of Greenland’s GDP .
“If every Greenland shark in Baffin Bay vanished tomorrow, the inshore fishery in Avannaata would still face too many boats working a quota under pressure, rising costs and no alternative employment,” he says. “When margins are narrow, a longstanding nuisance becomes intolerable.”
Even though the price of halibut continues to rise, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the average size of the fish is decreasing annually. While Jensen maintains he can still make a good living from fishing, he describes putting fewer hooks out and bringing in fewer fish, suggesting this is due to overfishing by offshore trawlers.
For some of those fishing these waters, however, the shark is not the leading cause of losing gear. “There are more and more ‘ghost lines’ and they are too heavy to pull up by the machine we use,” Jensen says. Ghost lines are discarded or lost gear that can get entangled with new lines, breaking equipment and trapping marine life.
Halibut Greenland, a cooperatively owned fish-processing company in Ilulissat, provides funds to clean up ghost gear in the area, which ONKN views as more effective than a shark cull. Poulsen also proposes a gear-loss compensation scheme, as well as funded trials of acoustic shark deterrents.
Rebekka Nygård Bak, an adviser to Greenland’s Ministry of Fisheries, Hunting, Agriculture and Self Sufficiency, suggests new bycatch-friendly equipment regulations could be a solution. She says a campaign for better bycatch reporting will also be key to any next steps.
For Poulsen, the sharks and those fishing these waters are two components of the same ecosystem, facing growing pressures in changing seas. “The shark is the visible, tangible version of a problem whose real drivers are structural,” he says.
